pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that in the first year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, from this time forward, king Mosiah having gone the way of all the earth, having warred a good warfare, walking uprightly before God, leaving none to reign in his stead; nevertheless he established laws, and they were acknowledged by the people; therefore they were obliged to abide by the laws which he had made.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 2:1-2 + 2 Chronicles 1:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The way of all the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and both are a leader's farewell on the point of death. “Reign in his stead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8, Solomon's word about succeeding David; the past-tense regnal formula “reigned in his stead” occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses, and 1 Chronicles 29:28 joins it to David's own death notice ('he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead').
provenance.significance: Both halves of Mosiah's obituary are David's, and the second is negated. The KJV's dying-king sentence is 'I go the way of all the earth' (1 Kings 2:2), spoken by David to the son who will succeed him; the KJV's succession sentence is 'made me to reign in his stead' (2 Chronicles 1:8), spoken by that son. Mosiah is given the first and denied the second: 'leaving none to reign in his stead.' The chapter that opens the reign of the judges opens by quoting the transfer of the crown in order to say that it did not happen, and the KJV supplies both the formula and the vacancy in it. What follows in 1 Kings 2:3 is the charge to keep the law, which is precisely what Alma 1:1 substitutes for an heir: 'nevertheless he established laws … therefore they were obliged to abide by the laws which he had made.'

links.note: 'King Mosiah having gone the way of all the earth … leaving none to reign in his stead.' The phrase entered the corpus at 2 Nephi 1:14 in Lehi's mouth and was adjudicated again at Mosiah 1:9 for Benjamin; it re-enters here for Mosiah's own death, in a new book and a new hand, and this time carries a second KJV succession formula with it. What makes the row more than a recurrence is the negation: the borrowed clause reports the end of Nephite kingship, and 1:14 will call Mosiah 'our last king'. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.
links.text: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;

provenance.other: “A good warfare” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 1:18, and “war a good warfare” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon has 'having warred a good warfare', which occurs nowhere in the KJV and is the participle of Paul's phrase.
provenance.significance: The clause Paul uses is a charge to a young minister, and its immediate sequel is the reason this chapter needs it: 'Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck: of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander' (1:19-20). 1 Timothy 1 is the KJV's chapter about a named teacher who wrecked the faith and was handed over for discipline. Alma 1 is about a named teacher who wrecked the faith and was handed over for execution. Mosiah dies with Timothy's charge on him in the same sentence that hands the office to a judge who must immediately try Nehor.

links.note: 'Having warred a good warfare, walking uprightly before God.' A KJV singleton in participial form, doing epitaph duty. The rest of the clause is generic — 'walketh uprightly' is five KJV verses, all wisdom-literature — so the borrowing is the warfare phrase alone, which is why the row is an allusion rather than a quotation.
links.text: This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in the first year of the reign of Alma in the judgment seat, there was a man brought before him to be judged; a man which was large, and was noted for his much strength;

and he had gone about among the people, preaching to them that which he termed to be the word of God, bearing down against the church; declaring unto the people that every priest and teacher had ought to become popular; and they ought not to labor with their own hands, but that they had ought to be supported by the people;

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 4:12, via Mosiah 18:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Working with our own hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:12, and “work with your own hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 4:11. Acts 20:34-35 supplies the second term of Nehor's proposition — 'these hands have ministered unto my necessities … so labouring ye ought to support the weak' — which is the only KJV passage that joins hand-labour to the word 'support'.
provenance.significance: Nehor's doctrine is Paul's practice stated backwards, clause for clause. Paul labours with his own hands and refuses support; Nehor teaches that teachers 'ought not to labor with their own hands, but … ought to be supported by the people'. Recover Acts 20 and the inversion sharpens: Paul's farewell at Miletus warns of men who will 'draw away disciples after them' (20:30) and answers them by pointing at his hands and disclaiming any man's 'silver, or gold, or apparel' (20:33). Alma 1:5-6 gives Nehor money and costly apparel, and 1:7 has him try to 'lead away the people of the church'. The chapter is running Paul's Miletus speech in negative.

links.note: 'They ought not to labor with their own hands, but … ought to be supported by the people.' Mosiah 18:24 adjudicated the positive form of this — Alma the elder commanding his priests to labour with their own hands for their support — and this is a new book putting the same Pauline phrase in the mouth of the man who denies it. The link is written in full rather than recorded as a recurrence because the second use is the argument: the phrase Alma legislated at Mosiah 18:24 is the phrase the first man tried under his son's law is condemned for contradicting. The 1830 'labor with their own hands' keeps 'own', which 1920 deletes; the modern text reads 'labor with their hands' and the contact with 1 Corinthians 4:12 is fainter there.
links.text: And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:

pericopes.text: and he also testified unto the people that all mankind should be saved at the last day, and that they need not fear nor tremble, but that they might lift up their heads and rejoice: for the Lord had created all men, and had also redeemed all men; and in the end, all men should have eternal life.

provenance.other: “Lift up your heads” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 24:7 and 24:9, where the heads are a gate's, and Luke 21:28, the only one addressed to people and the only one that supplies a reason — 'for your redemption draweth nigh'.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:28 stands in the Olivet discourse, and the head is lifted because redemption is near for those who endure; eight verses later the same speech tells the hearer to 'watch … and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape'. Nehor keeps the imperative, keeps redemption ('had also redeemed all men'), and deletes the condition: in his mouth the eschatological encouragement becomes a guarantee, and there is nobody left to be accounted worthy because everybody already is. That is exactly the reading of Luke 21 the chapter is built to refute, and Alma 1:30 will answer it with the sorting scene of Matthew 25.

links.note: 'They need not fear nor tremble, but … might lift up their heads and rejoice: for the Lord … had also redeemed all men.' The KJV's one place where people lift up their heads because redemption is at hand. Adjudicated in this corpus at Mosiah 7:18, where Limhi uses the same imperative with a political reason; here the reason is soteriological and it is a heresy. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion because the shared run is four words and the second half of Luke's sentence is paraphrased, not reproduced.
links.whyNot: Four words, and 'lift up your heads' is available from Psalm 24 as much as from Luke, though the Psalm is speaking to gates. Universal salvation preaching in 1820s America had a settled vocabulary of its own, and the sentence may reflect that rather than any single verse.
links.text: And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he did teach these things so much, that many did believe on his words, even so many that they began to support him and give him money;
and he began to be lifted up in the pride of his heart, and to wear very costly apparel; yea, and even began to establish a church, after the manner of his preaching.

provenance.other: “The pride of his heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 32:26, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, this one. 2 Chronicles 32:27 has 'exceeding much riches and honour' and treasuries 'for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones'; 32:29 has 'possessions of flocks and herds in abundance'. “Riches and honour” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and “flocks and herds” occurs in exactly seven, so neither is decisive alone — the argument is that all three sit within four verses of the singleton.
provenance.significance: The chapter's economics come from one page of Chronicles. Hezekiah's heart 'was lifted up' (32:25), he humbled himself 'for the pride of his heart' (32:26), and the narrator then itemises exceeding much riches and honour, silver and gold and precious things, and flocks and herds in abundance. Alma 1 distributes the same four items across three verses — Nehor 'lifted up in the pride of his heart' (1:6), false teachers preaching 'for the sake of riches and honor' (1:16), a church 'exceeding rich' with 'abundance of flocks, and herds … and of gold, and of silver, and of precious things' (1:29). The suppressed correspondence is the one Chronicles makes explicit and Alma does not have to: Hezekiah's wealth is the occasion of his pride, and the wrath is deferred only because he humbles himself. Alma 1:29-30 has the wealth and the humility together, and the reader who recovers 2 Chronicles 32 knows what happens when they come apart — which is what Alma 4:6-8 will report.

links.note: 'He began to be lifted up in the pride of his heart, and to wear very costly apparel.' A KJV singleton, and the only occurrence of the phrase in the Book of Mormon, borrowed for the corpus's first named heresiarch. The three further contacts at 1:16 and 1:29 are recorded here rather than as separate links because they belong to one page of the source; the register carries a cross-reference at 1:29.
links.text: Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass as he was going to preach to those who believed on his word, he met a man which belonged to the church of God, yea, even one of their teachers; and he began to contend with him sharply, that he might lead away the people of the church; but the man withstood him, admonishing him with the words of God.
Now the name of the man was Gideon; and it was him that was an instrument in the hands of God, in delivering the people of Limhi out of bondage.—

Now because Gideon withstood him with the words of God, he was wroth with Gideon, and drew his sword and began to smite him. Now Gideon being stricken with many years, therefore he was not able to withstand his blows, therefore he was slain by the sword;

provenance.other: “Drew his sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:51, Gethsemane, and “take the sword shall perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the next one.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one man who draws his sword draws it in defence of a teacher against those who come to arrest him, and is told in the following verse that 'all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword'. Alma 1 executes that sentence. Nehor draws the sword against a man who withstood him 'with the words of God', kills him, and is condemned to die — for priestcraft, Alma says, 'but hast endeavored to enforce it by the sword' (1:12). The suppressed half of the borrowing is Jesus's reply, and the narrative supplies it as a verdict.

links.note: 'He was wroth with Gideon, and drew his sword and began to smite him.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and it has been in this corpus once before, at Mosiah 19:4, where the man who drew the sword was Gideon himself. This is a new book, and it is not the narrator recycling a formula: the same three words that armed Gideon at Mosiah 19:4 are now the words for the sword drawn against him, and 1:8 pauses the narrative to make sure the reader knows it is the same Gideon. The reversal is the reason the link is written in full rather than filed as a recurrence.
links.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear.

pericopes.text: and the man who slew him was taken by the people of the church, and was brought before Alma, to be judged according to the crime which he had committed.
And it came to pass that he stood before Alma, and plead for himself with much boldness.

But Alma said unto him, Behold, this is the first time that priestcraft has been introduced among this people. And behold, thou art not only guilty of priestcraft, but hast endeavored to enforce it by the sword; and were priestcraft to be enforced among this people, it would prove their entire destruction.
And thou hast shed the blood of a righteous man, yea, a man which has done much good among this people; and were we to spare thee, his blood would come upon us for vengeance;

provenance.other: “A righteous man” occurs in exactly 12 KJV verses, so the phrase is not decisive; 2 Samuel 4:11 has 'a righteous person'. What is rare is the sentence's structure. The KJV's formula for blood incurred by failing to punish is Deuteronomy 19:10, 'and so blood be upon thee', immediately followed at 19:13 by 'thine eye shall not pity him'. Matthew 27:25's 'His blood be on us, and on our children' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and is the New Testament's inversion of the same idea — blood incurred by condemning rather than by sparing.
provenance.significance: 2 Samuel 4:9-12 is the KJV's one scene of a newly-made ruler passing a capital sentence on the killers of a righteous man, and the reason he gives is the one Alma gives: 'wicked men have slain a righteous person … shall I not therefore now require his blood of your hand?' David has just come to the throne; Alma is in the first year of the judgeship, trying the first case under a code its author did not live to administer. Recover Deuteronomy 19 and the legal logic is complete — a land that lets shed blood go unpunished takes the guilt onto itself — which is exactly why Alma frames the sentence as self-protection rather than retribution: 'were we to spare thee, his blood would come upon us for vengeance.' The suppressed third text is Matthew 27:25, where the crowd volunteers for the guilt Alma is refusing.
provenance.alternative: A general Pentateuchal blood-guilt formula (Deuteronomy 19:10, 21:8-9; Leviticus 20:9; Joshua 2:19), of which 2 Samuel 4:11 would be one instance rather than the source.

links.note: 'Thou hast shed the blood of a righteous man … were we to spare thee, his blood would come upon us for vengeance.' No clause is reproduced and no phrase is rare on its own; the case is that the whole judicial sentence — new ruler, righteous man slain, blood required of the judges if they spare — has one biblical precedent and Alma delivers it in that precedent's order. Filed as conceptual for that reason.
links.whyNot: Blood-guilt language is spread across the KJV and any of a dozen verses could stand behind the sentence. The single closest phrase, 'a righteous man', occurs in twelve verses and 2 Samuel 4:11 is not one of them. A reader who wants only verbal evidence should decline this row.
links.text: How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed? shall I not therefore now require his blood of your hand, and take you away from the earth?

pericopes.text: therefore thou art condemned to die, according to the law which has been given us by Mosiah, our last king; and they have been acknowledged by this people; therefore this people must abide by the law.

And it came to pass that they took him; and his name was Nehor; and they carried him upon the top of the hill Manti, and there he was caused, or rather did acknowledge, between the heavens and the earth, that what he had taught to the people was contrary to the word of God; and there he suffered an ignominious death.

provenance.other: “Between the heaven and the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 18:9. The inverted “between the earth and the heaven” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (1 Chronicles 21:16, Ezekiel 8:3, Zechariah 5:9), all of them visionary and none of them a death. The 1830 reads 'between the heavens and the earth', pluralising the first noun.
provenance.significance: The KJV knows one man suspended between heaven and earth, and he is Absalom — who 'stole the hearts of the men of Israel' (2 Samuel 15:6) by standing where they came for judgment, and who died hanging in an oak with darts through him. Nehor's whole offence is popularity: he teaches that 'every priest and teacher had ought to become popular' (1:3), gathers a following, and is executed on a hilltop in Absalom's posture, having first been made to confess. Read with 2 Samuel 18, the manner of the death is a verdict on the manner of the ministry, and the 'ignominious death' the verse names without describing is the one the KJV gives to a usurper who courted a people's affection.

links.note: 'They carried him upon the top of the hill Manti, and there he … did acknowledge, between the heavens and the earth, that what he had taught … was contrary to the word of God.' A KJV singleton in the singular; the 1830's plural 'heavens' is the only obstacle and it is the ordinary Book of Mormon plural. Deuteronomy 21:22-23's hanged malefactor is the legal background a reader may reach for instead, and it is recorded as an alternative, but it has no verbal contact with the clause.
links.whyNot: Five words, one of them differing in number, and the phrase is natural English for a hilltop execution witnessed from below. Nothing else in 1:15 touches the Absalom narrative, and the popularity theme is stated in the chapter rather than imported from 2 Samuel.
links.text: And Absalom met the servants of David. And Absalom rode upon a mule, and the mule went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak, and he was taken up between the heaven and the earth; and the mule that was under him went away.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless this did not put an end to the spreading of priestcraft through the land: for there was many which loved the vain things of the world, and they went forth preaching false doctrines; and this they did for the sake of riches and honor.

Nevertheless they durst not lie, if it were known, for fear of the law, for liars were punished; therefore they pretended to preach according to their belief: and now the law could have no power on any man for their belief.
And they durst not steal, for fear of the law; for such were punished; neither durst they rob, nor murder: for he that murdered was punished unto death.
But it came to pass that whosoever did not belong to the Church of God, began to persecute those that did belong to the Church of God, and had taken upon them the name of Christ;

yea, they did persecute them, and afflict them with all manner of words, and this because of their humility; because they were not proud in their own eyes, and because they did impart the word of God, one with another, without money and without price.

provenance.other: “Without money and without price” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:1. mediation-check.py against Revelation 22:17, the New Testament's nearest re-use of the invitation, returns one decisive point for Isaiah: the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's buying-and-selling language, not Revelation's 'water of life freely'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 55's second verse is the one the chapter needs: 'Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?' Alma 1 is about money spent on preaching — Nehor's hearers 'began to support him and give him money' (1:5) — and about labour, since the whole quarrel with priestcraft is whether teachers work with their hands. The five words the persecuted church is described by are the five words of the KJV's one offer of unbought bread, and the sentence Isaiah puts next to them indicts exactly the transaction the chapter has just narrated. The persecution is 'because of their humility'; the thing they do without charge is what Nehor charged for.

links.note: 'They did impart the word of God, one with another, without money and without price.' A five-word KJV singleton, unaltered. The phrase entered the corpus as part of Jacob's sixteen-word transcription at 2 Nephi 9:50 and returns here as a description rather than an invitation — a new book, a new voice, and the words now name a practice instead of offering one. Below Skousen's threshold on its own and not one of his thirty-six.
links.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

pericopes.text: Now there was a strict law among the people of the Church, that there should not any man, belonging to the Church, arise and persecute those that did not belong to the Church, and that there should be no persecution among themselves.
Nevertheless, there were many among them who began to be proud, and began to contend warmly with their adversaries, even unto blows; yea, they would smite one another with their fists.

provenance.other: “Fist” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Exodus 21:18, the law of assault — ‘if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist’ — and Isaiah 58:4, ‘to smite with the fist of wickedness’. Alma 1:22 has both of Exodus’s elements, the striving and the fist, and the reciprocal ‘smite one another’, which occurs in no KJV verse at all but is Exodus 21:18’s ‘one smite another’ made plural. “Strive together” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Exodus 21:18 and Deuteronomy 25:11 are the two legal ones.
provenance.significance: The chapter is about what a law can reach. Alma 1:17-18 has just explained that the law punishes lying, theft, robbery and murder but ‘could have no power on any man for their belief’, and 1:33 closes by exercising it, ‘every man suffering according to that which he had done’. The one KJV verse that legislates church members’ blows is Exodus 21:18-19, and it is the mildest sentence in the code: if the man does not die, the striker pays for the loss of his time and heals him, and is quit. So the Book of Mormon describes a brawl inside the church in the words of the one biblical statute that treats a brawl as a civil matter rather than a sin, in a chapter that has just executed a man for enforcing doctrine by the sword. The Isaiah 58 recovery runs alongside and points the other way: Isaiah’s fast is condemned because it is kept ‘for strife and debate’ and answered by dealing bread to the hungry and covering the naked (58:7) — which is what Alma 1:27 and 1:30 describe the faithful doing five verses later.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 58:4, the other fist verse, and the one a reader is likelier to reach for because its fist belongs to religious people. Its wording is further from the sentence: Isaiah has no reciprocal and no striving together, only 'the fist of wickedness'.

links.note: 'They would smite one another with their fists.' Two of the KJV's rarest assault terms in one clause, and the closer of the two fist verses is the statute rather than the prophet: Exodus 21:18's men strive together and one smites another with his fist. The catalogue takes Isaiah 58:4 as a second, live source rather than discarding it, because Isaiah 58:4-7 supplies the shape of the whole passage — strife inside the assembly, then the hungry fed and the naked clothed — and Alma 1:22-30 has that shape. The 1:27 and 1:30 items are recorded here rather than as separate links.
links.text: And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed:

pericopes.text: Now this was in the second year of the reign of Alma, and it was a cause of much affliction to the Church; yea, it was the cause of much trial with the Church;
for the hearts of many were hardened, and their names were blotted out, that they were remembered no more among the people of God. And also many withdrew themselves from among them.

Now this was a great trial to those that did stand fast in the faith; nevertheless, they were steadfast and immoveable in keeping the commandments of God, and they bore with patience the persecution which was heaped upon them.

provenance.other: “Stand fast in the faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 16:13. “Unmoveable” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 27:41 (of a grounded ship) and 1 Corinthians 15:58, which is also the source of 'stedfast' in the pair. The 1830 spells it 'immoveable', keeping the KJV's -eable; 1920 modernises to 'immovable'.
provenance.significance: Two Pauline imperatives from adjacent chapters land in one Book of Mormon sentence, and both come from the ends of their chapters, where Paul is closing. 1 Corinthians 15:58 grounds steadfastness in the resurrection — 'forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord' — and 16:13 pairs standing fast with 'quit you like men, be strong', an exhortation to a church that has just been told about a collection and about who is worth supporting. Alma 1's persecuted church is defined by labour that is not in vain and by refusing to be paid for preaching, which is what makes the pair fit rather than merely arrive together.

links.note: 'Those that did stand fast in the faith; nevertheless, they were steadfast and immoveable in keeping the commandments of God.' Two consecutive clauses, two KJV rarities, from 1 Corinthians 16:13 and 15:58 in reverse order. The 15:58 half was adjudicated at 1 Nephi 2:10 and again at Mosiah 5:15, where Benjamin quotes three of its terms consecutively; the addition here is 16:13, which has not been used in the corpus before and which is a KJV singleton. That is why the row is written in full at the head of a new book rather than filed as a recurrence.
links.text: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.

pericopes.text: And now when the priests left their labor, to impart the word of God unto the people, the people also left their labors to hear the word of God. And when the priest had imparted unto them the word of God, they all returned again diligently unto their labors; and the priest, not esteeming himself above his hearers; for the preacher was no better than the hearer, neither was the teacher any better than the learner: and thus they were all equal, and they did all labor, every man according to his strength;

provenance.route: Matthew 10:24 / Luke 6:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV's formula is 'The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord' (Matthew 10:24), with Luke 6:40 giving the first half alone. The only shared word with Alma 1:26 is 'above', in 'not esteeming himself above his hearers'; the rest is a parallel construction rather than a reproduced clause, which is why the row is an echo.
provenance.significance: Matthew 10:24 is a levelling sentence used to warn: the disciple is not above the master, therefore expect what the master got, and 10:25 completes it with Beelzebub. Alma 1:26 turns the same construction into a rule of church economy — preacher no better than hearer, teacher no better than learner, 'and thus they were all equal' — and the pair it drops is the one Matthew keeps, servant and lord. Isaiah 24:2's 'as with the people, so with the priest' is the OT levelling formula and is recorded as an alternative; it belongs to a chapter of judgment, where levelling is a threat, and Alma's is a commendation.

links.note: 'The preacher was no better than the hearer, neither was the teacher any better than the learner.' Two paired clauses in the KJV's teacher-and-taught construction, and the priest is said not to esteem himself 'above his hearers', which is Matthew's preposition. Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a: the verbal contact is one word, and the case rests on the shape of the sentence and its fit with a chapter about paid preaching.
links.whyNot: One shared word. Egalitarian clergy language was common in the 1820s and the construction is a natural way to say what the verse says; a reader who declines this row is not obliged to find another source for it.
links.text: The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord.

pericopes.text: and they did impart of their substance every man according to that which he had, to the poor, and the needy, and the sick, and the afflicted; and they did not wear costly apparel, yet they were neat and comely:
and thus they did establish the affairs of the Church: and thus they began to have continual peace again, notwithstanding all their persecutions.

And now because of the steadiness of the Church, they began to be exceeding rich; having abundance of all things whatsoever they stood in need; an abundance of flocks, and herds, and fatlings of every kind, and also abundance of grain, and of gold, and of silver, and of precious things; and abundance of silk and fine twined linen, and all manner of good homely cloth.

provenance.other: “Fine twined linen” occurs in exactly 20 KJV verses and every one of them is in Exodus, in the making of the tabernacle and the priestly vestments; the phrase occurs in no other biblical book. “Silk” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Ezekiel 16:10 and 16:13 join it to fine linen and to gold and silver, and Revelation 18:12 lists it among Babylon's merchandise. The 1830's 'fine twined' is hyphenated in 1920.
provenance.significance: If the phrase is felt at all, the church's prosperity is described in the vocabulary the KJV reserves for the fabric of the sanctuary — the curtains, the veil and the ephod. The two verses that would put silk beside it are Ezekiel 16:10-13, where God clothes Jerusalem in silk and fine linen and gold and silver, and Ezekiel 16 exists to say what she did with them. Both recoveries point the same way and neither is required by the wording.

links.note: 'Abundance of silk and fine twined linen, and all manner of good homely cloth.' Recorded at low confidence under CONVENTIONS §0a because the distributional fact is genuinely striking — a phrase confined in the whole KJV to the tabernacle — and because a reader who notices it will want the register to have noticed it too. The gold, silver, precious things, flocks and herds of this verse are adjudicated at 1:6 with 2 Chronicles 32:27-29 and are not counted here.
links.whyNot: 'Fine twined linen' is simply the KJV's English for a grade of cloth, and a writer reaching for expensive fabric has nowhere else to reach. There is no tabernacle in view at Alma 1:29, no priestly garment, and the sentence is a list of commodities. If this is a borrowing it is an unconscious one, and the row should be read as a note on the KJV's distribution rather than as a claim about dependence.
links.text: Moreover thou shalt make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen, and blue, and purple, and scarlet: with cherubims of cunning work shalt thou make them.

pericopes.text: And thus in their prosperous circumstances they did not send away any which was naked, or that was hungry, or that was athirst, or that was sick, or that had not been nourished; and they did not set their hearts upon riches; therefore they were liberal to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, whether out of the Church or in the Church, having no respects to persons as to those who stood in need;

provenance.other: Alma 1:30's list is naked, hungry, athirst, sick. Matthew 25:44's is 'an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison' — four of Alma's four terms, and it is the only KJV verse that puts them in one series. “Athirst” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and 25:44 is the only one in a judgment context; 25:35-36 and 25:43 give the same list distributed over two verses with 'thirsty' instead.
provenance.significance: The list is the criterion of the last judgment. Matthew 25:31-46 divides the nations by precisely these acts, and the sheep are those who did them. Alma 1 opened with Nehor preaching that 'all mankind should be saved at the last day' and that all should 'have eternal life' (1:4); it closes by describing a church that does the six things Matthew's last day sorts on. Nothing in the chapter argues against universal salvation. It answers it by narrating the works Matthew makes the test, and by putting them in the church Nehor tried to destroy. Matthew 25:46's own last words are 'life eternal', which is the phrase Nehor promised to everyone.

links.note: 'They did not send away any which was naked, or that was hungry, or that was athirst, or that was sick, or that had not been nourished.' No clause is reproduced, but four of Matthew's terms arrive as one series, including 'athirst', which the KJV uses in a judgment scene only here. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's 25:44 form ('athirst') rather than the 25:35 form ('thirsty').
links.text: Then shall they also answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?

provenance.other: “Respect of persons” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and “respecter of persons” occurs in exactly one (Acts 10:34), so the phrase alone is not decisive. What is unusual is the company it keeps here. James 2 is the one biblical chapter that runs the same four items in the same order: respect of persons (2:1), a rich man in 'goodly apparel' against a poor man in 'vile raiment' (2:2-3), and a brother or sister 'naked, and destitute of daily food' who is sent away with words and not with goods (2:15-16). 'Bond and free' with 'male and female' is Galatians 3:28's pairing, where the KJV reads 'neither bond nor free … neither male nor female'.
provenance.significance: James 2's argument is that faith without works is dead, and its worked example is a congregation that seats the well-dressed and dismisses the naked. Alma 1:27-32 is the same congregation described twice over: the faithful 'did not wear costly apparel' and did not send away the naked and the hungry; those outside are marked by 'wearing costly apparel'. The suppressed correspondence is James's conclusion, which the chapter does not state and does not need to — that the apparel and the sending away are the same sin, and that a profession which does neither of James's works is not a faith at all. That is also the answer to Nehor at 1:4.

links.note: 'They did not send away any which was naked … having no respects to persons as to those who stood in need.' The individual phrases are not rare; the sequence is. Costly apparel, respect of persons, and the naked and hungry sent away empty are James 2's three moves in James 2's order, distributed across Alma 1:27-32. The 'bond and free … male and female' pair is Galatians 3:28's, adjudicated in this corpus at 2 Nephi 10:16 and used here for church almsgiving rather than for baptism. Offered as a chapter-level dependence rather than a verse-level one, which is why the confidence is moderate.
links.whyNot: No clause is reproduced and every element can be sourced elsewhere: 'respect of persons' is eight KJV verses, 'costly array' is 1 Timothy 2:9, and clothing the naked is Isaiah 58:7, which this catalogue has already used at 1:22. The case is cumulative, and a reader who does not grant the cumulation has nothing left.
links.text: If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food,

pericopes.text: and thus they did prosper and become far more wealthy, than those who did not belong to their Church.

For those who did not belong to their Church, did indulge themselves in sorceries, and in idolatry or idleness, and in bablings, and in envyings and strife; wearing costly apparel; being lifted up in the pride of their own eyes; lying, thieving, robbing, commiting whoredoms, and murdering, and all manner of wickedness; nevertheless, the law was put in force upon all those who did transgress it, inasmuch as it were possible.

provenance.other: “Envyings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 5:21 and 2 Corinthians 12:20. “Babblings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16, both as “vain babblings”. Galatians 5:20-21 supplies idolatry, witchcraft, strife, envyings and murders in that order; Alma 1:32 has sorceries, idolatry, babblings, envyings and strife, whoredoms and murdering. Revelation 9:21 is the KJV's other list joining sorceries to murders and fornication.
provenance.significance: Galatians 5:19-21 is the KJV's works-of-the-flesh catalogue and it ends 'they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God'. Alma 1:32 assembles a list out of it and hands it to those outside the church, one verse after saying that the church prospered more than they did; and the verse ends not with exclusion from the kingdom but with 'the law was put in force upon all those who did transgress it'. The suppressed correspondence is the substitution: Paul's list is disqualifying before God, and the chapter that has spent seventeen verses insisting the law has 'no power on any man for their belief' (1:17) reprints his list under a civil magistrate. The two 'babblings' verses are Paul warning Timothy about talkers who suppose 'that gain is godliness' (1 Timothy 6:5), which is the chapter's definition of priestcraft.
provenance.alternative: A generic vice-list drawn from no single verse. The Book of Mormon has several, and the KJV has several to draw on.

links.note: 'Sorceries, and in idolatry or idleness, and in bablings, and in envyings and strife … lying, thieving, robbing, commiting whoredoms, and murdering.' Two of the list's terms are KJV rarities of two verses each, and one of the two pairs sits in Galatians 5:20-21. The 1830 spellings 'bablings' and 'commiting' are the first edition's; the point does not turn on them. Filed at moderate because vice-lists are the one genre where shared vocabulary proves least.
links.whyNot: Vice catalogues share words by definition, and the overlap with Galatians is four terms out of eleven with the order rearranged. 'Idolatry or idleness' is a peculiarity of the 1830 that no KJV list explains, and if the source were Galatians one would expect fornication and drunkenness rather than lying and thieving.
links.text: Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
Behold, this was the iniquity of thy sister Sodom, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness was in her and in her daughters, neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.

provenance.other: “Idleness” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Proverbs 31:27, Ecclesiastes 10:18, Ezekiel 16:49) and “abundance of idleness” occurs in exactly one. Ezekiel 16:49 is the only KJV verse that names idleness as a public sin, and it names it in a series — pride, fulness of bread, abundance of idleness, and a hand not strengthened for the poor and needy. The 1830's odd 'idolatry or idleness' is what puts the word here; 1920 keeps it.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16:49 is the KJV's definition of the sin of Sodom, and it is an economic one: pride, plenty, leisure, and no hand held out to the poor. Alma 1 is that verse's four items sorted into two peoples. The church has the plenty — 'exceeding rich', 'abundance' four times over at 1:29 — and answers it at 1:27 and 1:30 by imparting substance to the poor and the needy and sending none away hungry. Those outside have the pride ('lifted up in the pride of their own eyes', the same verse) and the idleness, and the chapter's last word on them is that the law had to be put in force. Recover Ezekiel 16 and a second thing follows: 16:13's silk and fine linen and gold and silver are the wealth God gave Jerusalem before she misused it, and Alma 1:29's inventory is the same list. The chapter is being measured against the verse that says wealth without almsgiving is Sodom.
provenance.alternative: A vice list assembled from no single source; the Galatians 5:19-21 link at this verse is the alternative account of where its terms come from, and the two are not exclusive.

links.note: 'Did indulge themselves in sorceries, and in idolatry or idleness … being lifted up in the pride of their own eyes.' The word that carries the row is 'idleness', which the KJV uses three times and only once of a nation, in a verse that also supplies pride, abundance, and the poor and needy — all three of which Alma 1 uses within six verses. No clause is reproduced, so the row is conceptual; what makes it more than thematic is that the source verse is a list and the borrowing takes four of its four items.
links.whyNot: Not one phrase is shared. 'Idleness' is a common English word whose KJV rarity may be an accident of the translators' vocabulary rather than a signal, and pride, abundance and care for the poor are the Book of Mormon's own standing themes from 2 Nephi onward. The cumulative case is the whole case.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that by thus exercising the law upon them, every man suffering according to that which he had done, they became more still, and durst not commit any wickedness, if it were known; therefore, there was much peace among the people of Nephi, until the fifth year of the reign of the judges.

And it came to pass in the commencement of the fifth year of their reign, there began to be a contention among the people, for a certain man, being called Amlici; he being a very cunning man, yea, a wise man, as to the wisdom of the world; he being after the order of the man that slew Gideon by the sword, who was executed according to the law.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 3:19, via Mosiah 24:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The wisdom of this world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6 and 3:19, and nowhere else; “the wisdom of the world” occurs in no KJV verse, so the Book of Mormon has dropped Paul's demonstrative in both of its uses of the formula. Alma 2:1's is the second, after Mosiah 24:7.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 3:19 does not stop at calling the world's wisdom foolishness. It goes on: 'For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness' — the KJV's rendering of Job 5:13. Alma 2:1 introduces Amlici as 'a very cunning man, yea, a wise man, as to the wisdom of the world', and the chapter then takes him in his own craftiness: the cunning that draws away much people gets him made king by his own faction, marched against his brethren, and killed in single combat by the judge he tried to replace. The unstated half of the borrowed phrase is the sentence that predicts the plot.

links.note: 'He being a very cunning man, yea, a wise man, as to the wisdom of the world.' Paul's phrase, used as a verdict rather than a description, exactly as Mosiah 24:7 used it of the Lamanites — 'a cunning and a wise people, as to the wisdom of the world'. This is a new book and a new subject, an individual rather than a nation, but the formula is identical down to the 'as to' that does the disqualifying, and it is Alma 2's first characterisation of the man the chapter exists to bury. Recorded as a fresh link rather than a recurrence for the reason ADJUDICATING §4 gives for book boundaries.
links.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

pericopes.text: Now this Amlici had, by his cunning, drawn away much people after him; even so much that they began to be very powerful; and they began to endeavor to establish Amlici to be a king over the people.

provenance.other: “Drew away much people after him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:37, and the shorter “much people after him” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 2:2 has 'drawn away much people after him' — five consecutive words, with only the participle changed. The corpus's other borrowing from this family is Acts 20:30's “draw away disciples” (also a KJV singleton), adjudicated at Mosiah 29:7.
provenance.significance: Gamaliel's speech is a test, and Alma 2 applies it. Acts 5:36-39 offers two precedents — Theudas, 'who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered', and Judas of Galilee, who 'drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed' — and draws the rule: 'if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.' Alma 2 narrates the borrowed clause's own sequel. Amlici draws away much people after him (2:2), is slain by Alma with the sword (2:31), and his followers are scattered and driven into the wilderness (2:37) — slain, scattered, come to nought, in Gamaliel's order. The chapter does not cite the rule; it borrows the example and then supplies the outcome the example was quoted to establish.
provenance.alternative: Acts 20:30, the other KJV singleton in this family, which the corpus has already used at Mosiah 29:7.

links.note: Five consecutive words of a KJV singleton, altered only in the tense of the verb. What earns the row beyond the run is that Mosiah 29:7 predicted this event in the *other* singleton — 'draw away a part of this people after him', which is Acts 20:30's construction — and Alma 2:2 reports it in Gamaliel's. The warning is Paul's and the fulfilment is Luke's, and the two are two verses apart in the KJV's own vocabulary for schism. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; recorded as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length.
links.text: After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.

pericopes.text: Now this was alarming to the people of the Church, and also to all those who had not been drawn away after the persuasions of Amlici: for they knew that according to their law that such things must be established by the voice of the people;

therefore, if it were possible that Amlici should gain the voice of the people, he being a wicked man, would deprive them of their rights and privileges of the Church, &c: for it was his intent to destroy the Church of God.

And it came to pass that the people assembled themselves together throughout all the land, every man according to his mind, whether it were for or against Amlici, in separate bodies, having much dispute and wonderful contentions one with another;
and thus they did assemble themselves together, to cast in their voices concerning the matter: and they were laid before the judges.
And it came to pass that the voice of the people came against Amlici, that he was not made king over the people.

provenance.other: “Voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, God's concession to Samuel: 'Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me.' Alma 2 uses the phrase four times in five verses (2:3, 2:4, 2:6, 2:7).
provenance.significance: The phrase reverses direction here, and that is the finding. In 1 Samuel 8 the voice of the people is a demand for a king and God grants it as a rejection of himself; at Mosiah 29:2 it was that demand almost verbatim, a people asking an ageing ruler for a king out of his own sons. At Alma 2:7 the same phrase refuses one: 'the voice of the people came against Amlici, that he was not made king over the people.' Two chapters after Mosiah abolished the monarchy on the argument that the voice of the people rarely desires what is wrong, the institution he built out of Israel's worst decision makes the opposite decision in Israel's own words. The unstated correspondence is that 1 Samuel 8 supplies both the mechanism and the warning, and Alma 2:9 immediately shows the warning was sound: the losing faction consecrates Amlici king anyway.
provenance.alternative: 1 Samuel 8:19-20, where the people refuse Samuel's voice and insist on a king 'like all the nations', which is closer to what Amlici's faction then does at 2:9.

links.note: 'The voice of the people came against Amlici, that he was not made king over the people.' A KJV singleton, and the corpus's fourth substantial use of it — 2 Nephi 10:11, Mosiah 7:9, Mosiah 29:2 — but the first in which it decides a question the other way. Written in full rather than recorded as a recurrence for both of ADJUDICATING §4's reasons: this is a new book, and the second use is itself the argument, since the passage the phrase first translated is the passage now being answered.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: Now this did cause much joy in the hearts of those which were against him; but Amlici did stir up those which were in his favor, to anger against those which were not in his favor.
And it came to pass that they gathered themselves together, and did consecrate Amlici to be their king.
Now when Amlici was made king over them, he commanded them that they should take up arms against their brethren; and this he done, that he might subject them to him.
Now the people of Amlici were distinguished by the name of Amlici, being called Amlicites; and the remainder were called Nephites, or the people of God;

therefore the people of the Nephites was aware of the intent of the Amlicites, and therefore they did prepare for to meet them; yea, they did arm themselves with swords, and with cimeters, and with bows, and with arrows, and with stones, and with slings, and with all manner of weapons of war, of every kind;
and thus they were prepared to meet the Amlicites at the time of their coming. And there was appointed captains, and higher captains, and chief captains, according to their numbers.
And it came to pass that Amlici did arm his men with all manner of weapons of war, of every kind; and he also appointed rulers and leaders over his people, to lead them to war against their brethren.
And it came to pass that the Amlicites came up upon the hill Amnihu, which was east of the river Sidon, which ran by the land of Zarahemla, and there they began to make war with the Nephites.

Now Alma, he being the chief judge, and the governor of the people of Nephi, therefore he went up with his people, yea, with his captains, and chief captains, yea, at the head of his armies, against the Amlicites to battle;

and they began to slay the Amlicites upon the hill east of Sidom. And the Amlicites did contend with the Nephites with great strength, insomuch that many of the Nephites did fall before the Amlicites;
nevertheless the Lord did strengthen the hand of the Nephites, that they slew the Amlicites with a great slaughter, that they began to flee before them.

And it came to pass that the Nephites did pursue the Amlicites all that day, and did slay them with much slaughter, insomuch that there was slain of the Amlicites twelve thousand five hundred thirty and two souls; and there was slain of the Nephites, six thousand five hundred sixty and two souls.

And it came to pass that when Alma could pursue the Amlicites no longer, he caused that his people should pitch their tents in the valley of Gideon, the valley being called after that Gideon which was slain by the hand of Nehor with the sword; and in this valley the Nephites did pitch their tents for the night.

And Alma sent spies to follow the remnant of the Amlicites, that he might know of their plans and their plots, whereby he might guard himself against them, that he might preserve his people from being destroyed.

Now those which he had sent out to watch the camp of the Amlicites, were called Zeram, and Amnor, and Manti, and Limher; these were they which went out with their men to watch the camp of the Amlicites.
And it came to pass that on the morrow they returned into the camp of the Nephites, in great haste, being greatly astonished, and struck with much fear, saying,

Behold, we followed the camp of the Amlicites, and to our great astonishment, in the land of Minon, above the land of Zarahemla, in the course of the land of Nephi, we saw a numerous host of the Lamanites; and behold, the Amlicites have joined them,

and they are upon our brethren in that land; and they are fleeing before them with their flocks, and their wives, and their children, towards our city; and except we make haste, they obtain possession of our city; and our fathers, and our wives, and our children be slain.

provenance.other: “Our wives and our children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:3 — 'that our wives and our children should be a prey'. The Book of Mormon has 'our fathers, and our wives, and our children be slain'. The surrounding scene is Numbers 13's as well: spies sent to view a land (13:2, 13:17), a return with a report of 'men of a great stature' (13:32), and a night of weeping.
provenance.significance: This is the KJV's spy-report scene, and the Book of Mormon corrects it. In Numbers the returning spies bring 'an evil report' and the people's cry about their wives and children is the faithless sentence that costs Israel forty years and a generation. In Alma 2 the spies are named (2:22), their report is true, and the cry is an accurate alarm that produces the right action: the camp breaks, crosses Sidon, prays, and wins. The unstated correspondence is the verdict Numbers 14 pronounces on the sentence Alma 2:25 borrows — and the difference is not the report but what the hearers do next. Numbers 14:3 ends 'were it not better for us to return into Egypt?'; Alma 2:26 has the people go towards their city instead.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 20:13's 'their little ones, their wives, and their children', where Judah stands before the LORD before a battle against a great multitude — thematically nearer to Alma 2:28's prayer, but its possessive is third-person and it is not a spy report.

links.note: 'Our fathers, and our wives, and our children be slain.' A KJV singleton phrase arriving inside a reproduction of the scene it belongs to: spies sent out (2:21), spies named (2:22), spies returning in fear on the morrow (2:23), a report of a numerous host seen with 'great astonishment' (2:24), then the cry for the wives and the children. The machine ranked Numbers 14:3 on the shared run without seeing the type-scene around it.
links.text: And wherefore hath the LORD brought us unto this land, to fall by the sword, that our wives and our children should be a prey? were it not better for us to return into Egypt?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people of Nephi took their tents, and departed out of the valley of Gideon towards their city, which was the city of Zarahemla.
And behold, as they were crossing the river Sidon, the Lamanites and the Amlicites, being as numerous almost, as it were, as the sands of the sea, came upon them to destroy them;

provenance.other: “As the sand” occurs in exactly 18 KJV verses; the simile is common and no single verse owns it. Three of the eighteen apply it to an enemy army — Judges 7:12 (the Midianites, 'as the sand by the sea side for multitude'), Joshua 11:4 and 1 Samuel 13:5 — and one, Genesis 22:17, is the promise to Abraham's seed. The Book of Mormon's 'the sands of the sea' matches no KJV verse exactly.
provenance.significance: Seven verses earlier the narrator stopped the battle to explain a place-name: the army pitches 'in the valley of Gideon, the valley being called after that Gideon which was slain by the hand of Nehor' (2:20). The KJV has one Gideon and one valley, and in that valley the enemy lie 'as the sand by the sea side for multitude' (Judges 7:12) and are beaten by three hundred men, precisely so that Israel cannot 'vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me' (7:2). Alma 2:27-28 has the sand-multitude come up out of the valley of Gideon's camp, and its next sentence gives the victory to the hand of the Lord rather than to numbers. The further recovery is uglier and is the reason the row is worth writing: Genesis 22:17 made the sand of the sea a promise about Abraham's seed, and the sand-multitude here is the Lamanites, who are that seed.
provenance.alternative: A stock biblical simile for an innumerable host, used without reference to any one verse.

links.note: 'Being as numerous almost, as it were, as the sands of the sea.' The simile is common and the row does not rest on it. It rests on the narrator having just named the ground after Gideon and explained the name, three verses before deploying the simile that the KJV's Gideon narrative uses for the enemy he faced in a valley. Filed as conceptual and at moderate for that reason.
links.whyNot: 'As the sand' is one of the KJV's most widely distributed similes and the Book of Mormon uses it elsewhere without a Judges context. The valley of Gideon is named for a Nephite Gideon, not for the judge, and the text says so explicitly at 2:20 — which cuts both ways, since it shows the narrator thinking about the name at exactly this point.
links.text: And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like grasshoppers for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand by the sea side for multitude.

pericopes.text: nevertheless the Nephites, being strengthened by the hand of the Lord, having prayed mightily to him that he would deliver them out of the hands of their enemies; therefore the Lord did hear their cries, and did strengthen them, and the Lamanites and the Amlicites did fall before them.

provenance.other: “Out of the hand of their enemies” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 2:18 and Nehemiah 9:27, and both are statements of the judges cycle; the Book of Mormon's plural 'out of the hands of their enemies' occurs in none. “Heard their cry” occurs in exactly three (Exodus 3:7, Nehemiah 5:6, Psalm 106:44). The machine ranked Judges 2:14, the same passage's opposite half — Israel sold 'into the hands of their enemies'.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:11-19 is the KJV's programmatic statement of what a judge is for: the people are sold into the hand of their enemies, they cry, the LORD raises up judges, and he 'delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge'. Alma 2 is the first war of a nation that has just replaced its kings with judges, fought by a chief judge in person, and it resolves in that formula's terms — a cry, a hand, a deliverance. Nehemiah 9:27 states the same cycle retrospectively and adds the word Alma 2:28 needs: 'when they cried unto thee, thou heardest them from heaven … thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies.' What the Book of Mormon does not take from Judges 2 is its last clause, that the people relapsed as soon as the judge died — and Alma 4 will supply it.

links.note: 'Having prayed mightily to him that he would deliver them out of the hands of their enemies; therefore the Lord did hear their cries.' No clause is reproduced; two KJV rarities are, and they belong to the passage that defines the office Alma holds. Filed at moderate as conceptual because the deliverance formula is spread widely enough across the KJV that no single verse is compelled.
links.whyNot: Deliverance from the hand of enemies is among the KJV's commonest theological sentences and the Book of Mormon has used versions of it since 1 Nephi. The plural 'hands' matches no KJV verse, and the argument depends on the reader granting that the reign of the judges makes Judges 2 relevant.
links.text: And when the LORD raised them up judges, then the LORD was with the judge, and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge: for it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma fought with Amlici with the sword, face to face; and they did contend mightily, one with another.

And it came to pass that Alma, he being a man of God, being exercised with much faith, and he cried, saying, O Lord, have mercy and spare my life, that I may be an instrument in thy hands, to save and preserve this people.

provenance.other: “To save your lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:7, and “to preserve life” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 45:5. Alma 2:30 has 'to save and preserve this people' — both of Joseph's verbs, in Joseph's order, with 'this people' for the lives and the posterity. The pairing is nearly confined in the KJV to this one speech; Genesis 50:20 restates it as 'to save much people alive'.
provenance.significance: Joseph's disclosure to his brothers is the KJV's one place where a man asks to be understood as God's means of preserving his own kindred from destruction — 'God did send me before you to preserve life' — and the brothers he says it to are the ones who sold him. Alma prays it in the middle of single combat against a man whose army is his own people's brethren, and the corpus has used the same speech twice before: 2 Nephi 3:16 makes it a promise about Joseph's seed, and 1 Nephi 5:14 reaches it through Stephen. What Alma adds is the instrument. He does not ask to be preserved; he asks to be 'an instrument in thy hands', which is the phrase Alma 1:8 used of the Gideon whose valley he has just camped in and whose killer's heir he is now fighting.

links.note: 'O Lord, have mercy and spare my life, that I may be an instrument in thy hands, to save and preserve this people.' Two KJV singletons from one speech, reduced to their verbs. Filed at moderate rather than high because both verbs are ordinary English and only their pairing is rare; the corpus's earlier use of the same speech at 2 Nephi 3:16 was filed at moderate for the same reason.
links.whyNot: 'Save' and 'preserve' are common words and a prayer for a people's deliverance could reach them without Genesis. Nothing else in Alma 2 is Josephan, and the Joseph-in-Egypt frame the corpus uses elsewhere is not invoked here.
links.text: And God sent me before you to preserve you a posterity in the earth, and to save your lives by a great deliverance.

pericopes.text: Now when Alma had said these words, he contended again with Amlici; and he was strengthened, insomuch that he slew Amlici with the sword.
And he also contended with the king of the Lamanites; but the king of the Lamanites fled back from before Alma, and sent his guards to contend with Alma.
But Alma, with his guards, contended with the guards of the king of the Lamanites, until he slew and drove them back;

and thus he cleared the ground, or rather the bank, which was on the west of the river Sidon, throwing the bodies of the Lamanites which had been slain, into the waters of Sidon, that thereby his people might have room to cross and contend with the Lamanites and the Amlicites, on the west side of the river Sidon.

And it came to pass that when they had all crossed the river Sidon, that the Lamanites and the Amlicites began to flee before them, notwithstanding they were so numerous that they could not be numbered;
and they fled before the Nephites, towards the wilderness which was west and north, away beyond the borders of the land; and the Nephites did pursue them with their might, and did slay them;

yea, they were met on every hand, and slain, and driven, until they were scattered on the west, and on the north, until they had reached the wilderness, which was called Hermounts; and it was that part of the wilderness which was infested by wild and ravenous beasts.

And it came to pass that many died in the wilderness of their wounds, and were devoured by those beasts, and also the vultures of the air; and their bones have been found, and have been heaped up on the earth.

provenance.other: “Ravenous birds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:4, and “ravenous beast” occurs in exactly one, Isaiah 35:9; the Book of Mormon's plural 'ravenous beasts' occurs in neither. “To be devoured” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Ezekiel 39:4 is one. “Man's bone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:15. “Vulture” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Leviticus 11:14, Deuteronomy 14:13, Job 28:7), none of them a battlefield: the KJV's carrion birds are always 'fowls of the air'.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 39 is the KJV's one extended account of what becomes of a defeated multitude's bodies, and Alma 2:37-38 uses it in sequence. Ezekiel gives Gog's host 'unto the ravenous birds of every sort, and to the beasts of the field to be devoured' (39:4); the Book of Mormon splits that pair, moves the adjective onto the beasts — 'wild and ravenous beasts' at 2:37 — and supplies a bird of its own, the vulture, which the KJV never uses this way. Ezekiel then spends 39:11-15 on the bones: a valley of burial, seven months of searching, and a man who sets up a sign wherever he sees a bone. Alma 2:38 ends 'their bones have been found, and have been heaped up on the earth' — found and left unburied, which is the one thing Ezekiel's chapter exists to prevent. The suppressed correspondence is a refusal: Ezekiel's slaughter is cleansed from the land and Amlici's is not.

links.note: 'Many died in the wilderness of their wounds, and were devoured by those beasts, and also the vultures of the air; and their bones have been found, and have been heaped up on the earth.' No clause is reproduced, but three of the passage's terms are KJV rarities and one of them, 'ravenous', is a singleton that has been moved from the birds to the beasts in the preceding verse. 'Vultures of the air' is the KJV's 'fowls of the air' formula with a word substituted that the KJV uses only in dietary lists — a departure worth recording as such.
links.text: Thou shalt fall upon the mountains of Israel, thou, and all thy bands, and the people that is with thee: I will give thee unto the ravenous birds of every sort, and to the beasts of the field to be devoured.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Nephites, which were not slain by the weapons of war, after having buried those which had been slain: now the number of the slain were not numbered, because of the greatness of their number; and after they had finished burying their dead, they all returned to their lands, and to their houses, and their wives, and their children.

Now many women and children had been slain with the sword, and also many of their flocks and their herds; and also many of their fields of grain were destroyed, for they were trodden down by the hosts of men.

And now as many of the Lamanites and the Amlicites which had been slain upon the bank of the river Sidon, were cast into the waters of Sidon; and behold, their bones are in the depths of the sea, and they are many.—

provenance.other: “Dead upon the sea shore” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 14:30, and “the depths have covered” occurs in exactly one, Exodus 15:5. “Depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10 and Micah 7:19 — and not one of them holds a body; Micah's holds forgiven sins. The Book of Mormon puts bones there, and puts them in a river.
provenance.significance: Alma 2:34 is the sentence this verse completes: Alma clears the bank by 'throwing the bodies of the Lamanites which had been slain, into the waters of Sidon, that thereby his people might have room to cross', and at 2:35 'they had all crossed the river Sidon'. That is Exodus 14 with the order reversed — Israel crosses and then sees the Egyptians dead in the water; the Nephites make the dead in the water the condition of crossing. Alma 3:3 then names the resting place with Micah's phrase, which in the KJV is where God puts sins he has decided to forget, and adds the one detail Ezekiel 39 spent five verses preventing: the bones are still there. The two recoveries pull against each other, and the chapter that follows is about a mark that cannot be washed off.

links.note: 'Their bones are in the depths of the sea, and they are many.' No clause is reproduced and the phrase itself belongs to Micah rather than to Exodus; the row is filed on the shape of the episode, which is a body of water made passable by the corpses of a drowned army. Filed at moderate and as conceptual for that reason. The oddity worth recording on its own is the geography: Sidon is a river throughout Alma, and this verse calls its depths the depths of the sea.
links.whyNot: The KJV's sea-depths language is spread over four books and Alma 3:3 shares no run of more than three words with any of them. A narrator disposing of bodies in a river might reach for 'the depths' without Exodus, and the Exodus reading depends on the previous chapter rather than on this verse.
links.text: Thus the LORD saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians; and Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore.

pericopes.text: And the Amlicites were distinguished from the Nephites, for they had marked themselves with red in their foreheads, after the manner of the Lamanites; nevertheless they had not shorn their heads like unto the Lamanites.

Now the heads of the Lamanites were shorn; and they were naked, save it were skin, which was girded about their loins, and also their armour, which was girded about them, and their bows, and their arrows, and their stones, and their slings, &c.

And the skins of the Lamanites were dark, according to the mark which was set upon their fathers, which was a curse upon them because of their transgression and their rebellion against their brethren, which consisted of Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam, which were just and holy men.

provenance.other: “The skins of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 27:16, where Rebekah puts the skins of the kids of the goats on Jacob's hands and neck. “A hairy man” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 27:11. Genesis 25:25 has the elder twin born 'red, all over like an hairy garment'. The n-gram stream ranked Genesis 27:16 on the four-word run without seeing what surrounds it.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one story in which skin is used to tell two brothers apart, and it is the story in which the telling fails. Esau is the elder, red and hairy; Jacob is the younger and smooth; the skins of goats are laid on the younger's hands so that a blind father will feel the elder and give away the birthright. Alma 3 is that story's premise made permanent. Two brothers' descendants are distinguished by skin (3:6), by hair — the Lamanites' heads 'were shorn' and the Amlicites' were not (3:4-5) — and by red laid on the body (3:4, 3:13), and the point of the whole apparatus is that the seed of the elder brothers must not be mistaken for the seed of the younger. Recover Genesis 27 and the mark is doing what Rebekah's goatskins did, in reverse and by decree: making the difference between brothers legible on the skin so that the blessing cannot go to the wrong one. The Book of Mormon's younger brothers are named in this very verse — Nephi, Jacob, Joseph and Sam.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 27:16 as an unmeaning four-word coincidence, the skins in Alma 3:6 being simply the ordinary word for human skin.

links.note: 'And the skins of the Lamanites were dark, according to the mark which was set upon their fathers.' Four words of a KJV singleton, and on its own that is a coincidence worth nothing. What makes the row is the company: within two verses on either side Alma 3 has hair (3:4, 3:5), red on the body (3:4), skin as a token of which brother's seed a man belongs to (3:6-8), and at 3:14 the oracle of separation from Genesis 25:23, which is adjudicated at that verse. The Jacob-and-Esau complex is being used, and this verse is where its rarest phrase surfaces. Filed at moderate and as conceptual.
links.whyNot: 'The skins of the' is four common words and the KJV's single occurrence of the string is an accident of how often it writes 'skin' with a following genitive. There is no deception in Alma 3, no blessing, no blind father, and the direction of the typology is inverted — Genesis 27's skins conceal identity and Alma 3's mark reveals it.
links.text: And she put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck:

pericopes.text: And their brethren sought to destroy them; therefore they were cursed; and the Lord God set a mark upon them, yea, upon Laman and Lemuel, and also the sons of Ishmael, and the Ishmaelitish women:

provenance.route: Genesis 4:15 + Ezekiel 9:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Set a mark upon” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and Alma 3 uses both. Genesis 4:15 is 'the LORD set a mark upon Cain', which Alma 3:7 reproduces with the divine name changed — 'the Lord God set a mark upon them'. Ezekiel 9:4 is 'set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh', the KJV's only marked foreheads outside Revelation, and the foreheads are what Alma 3:4 and 3:13 supply. The phrase recurs five more times in this chapter (3:10, 3:13, 3:14, 3:15, 3:16).
provenance.significance: Both of the KJV's set marks protect, and Alma 3's separates. Genesis 4:15 marks Cain so that no one finding him should kill him — a mark given to a cursed man as a restraint on other men's violence; Ezekiel 9:4 marks the mourners in Jerusalem so that the slaughtering angels will 'come not near any man upon whom is the mark' (9:6). Alma 3:8 gives the Book of Mormon's reason and it is neither: the mark exists 'that their seed might be distinguished from the seed of their brethren', so that the two peoples will not mix. The suppressed correspondence is what the Genesis mark was for. Cain's cursing is a cursing from the earth and a sentence of wandering, and the mark is the mercy attached to it — the one thing that keeps the curse from becoming a death sentence. Alma 3:14 keeps the mercy as a clause ('except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me, that I may have mercy upon them') and 3:19 keeps Cain's other half, that a cursed man brings the condemnation on himself.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 4 alone, with the foreheads coming from Revelation 13:16 rather than from Ezekiel 9:4. The Revelation contact is adjudicated separately at 3:13.

links.note: 'The Lord God set a mark upon them, yea, upon Laman and Lemuel.' Four words of a two-verse KJV phrase, with the subject unchanged: in both of the KJV's uses it is the LORD who sets it, and in the Book of Mormon's it is the Lord God. The chapter is built on the phrase — it recurs at 3:10, 3:13, 3:14, 3:15 and 3:16, twice as a divine first-person promise — and the second KJV verse supplies the body part the first one lacks. Hardy's apparatus carries no row at Alma 3; the Cain background is standard in the discussion of these verses and is recorded as the catalogue's own reading rather than as anyone's.
links.text: And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.

pericopes.text: and this was done, that their seed might be distinguished from the seed of their brethren, that thereby the Lord God might preserve his people, that they might not mix and believe in incorrect traditions, which would prove their destruction.
And it came to pass that whosoever did mingle his seed with that of the Lamanites, did bring the same curse upon his seed;

provenance.route: Ezra 9:1-2, with Daniel 2:43 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Mingled themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezra 9:2 — 'the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands' — and “mingle themselves with the seed” occurs in exactly one, Daniel 2:43. “Holy seed” occurs in exactly two, Ezra 9:2 and Isaiah 6:13. Between them these two verses hold every element of Alma 3:9's sentence: the verb, the seed, and the mixing of peoples.
provenance.significance: 2 Nephi 5:23 stated this law first — 'cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed' — and stated it with a verb the KJV does not have: the King James Bible never writes 'mixeth'. Alma 3:9 says the same thing and puts the KJV's own verb back: 'whosoever did mingle his seed with that of the Lamanites'. That is what makes this a fresh link rather than a recurrence — the corpus has returned to the source and picked up the word it missed. Recover Ezra 9 and the rationale follows too. Ezra's crisis is that 'the people of Israel … have not separated themselves from the people of the lands', and the offence is defined by descent rather than by conduct; Alma 3:8 gives the identical reason in the identical order, separation of seed first and belief second, 'that they might not mix and believe in incorrect traditions'. The catalogue records without softening it that the KJV verse behind Alma 3:8-9 is the one that made Judah put away its foreign wives and children.

links.note: 'Whosoever did mingle his seed with that of the Lamanites, did bring the same curse upon his seed.' Two KJV singletons, one supplying the verb with its reflexive and one supplying its object. The corpus's earlier statement of the rule at 2 Nephi 5:23 was adjudicated against the same two verses at moderate, on a non-KJV verb; the verb here is Ezra's, which is why this row is written in full and at high.
links.text: For they have taken of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands: yea, the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass.

pericopes.text: therefore whomsoever suffered himself to be led away by the Lamanites, were called under that head, and there was a mark set upon him.

And it came to pass that whosoever would not believe in the tradition of the Lamanites, but believed those records which were brought out of the land of Jerusalem, and also in the tradition of their fathers, which were correct, which believed in the commandments of God, and kept them, were called the Nephites, or the people of Nephi, from that time forth;
and it is they which have kept the records which are true of their people, and also of the people of the Lamanites.
