Alma has already given that answer, at 14:11 — 'he doth suffer that they may do this thing … that the judgments which he shall exercise upon them in his wrath, may be just.' The chapter puts Pilate's question and John's answer eight verses apart and never names either.

links.note: 'Why do ye not answer the words of this people? Know ye not that I have power to deliver ye up unto the flames? And he commanded them to speak; but they answered nothing.' Six words in the frame of one of two KJV verses, and the other of the two is not an accusation. The n-gram stream ranked John 19:10 first here and was right; what reading supplies is the answer at John 19:11, which the Book of Mormon has already given at 14:11.
links.text: Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they departed and went their ways, but came again on the morrow; and the Judge also smote them again on their cheeks. And many came forth also, and smote them, saying: Will ye stand again and Judge this people, and condemn our law? If ye have such great power, why do ye not deliver yourselves?
And many such things did they say unto them, gnashing their teeth upon them, and spitting upon them, and saying, How shall we look when we are damned?

provenance.other: “gnashed on him with their teeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:54. The distinction matters because the KJV's other gnashing is a different idiom entirely: 'gnashing of teeth' occurs in seven verses, all of them the formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' for the torment of the damned, and none of them an act performed BY a mob UPON a person. Alma 14:21 has the Acts idiom — 'gnashing their teeth upon them, and spitting upon them'.
provenance.significance: Stephen's death is the New Testament's model martyrdom and Alma 14 has taken it in two pieces. The gnashing is here; the rest was at 14:7, where those who believed are cast out and men are sent to cast stones at them — Acts 7:58's 'cast him out of the city, and stoned him'. What the Book of Mormon adds is the taunt, 'How shall we look when we are damned?', and the addition is where the two gnashings meet: the men of Ammonihah gnash their teeth in the manner of Acts 7:54, and the phrase 'gnashing of teeth' everywhere else in the KJV names what will be done to them for it. They are quoting their own sentence and they know it, which is why the sentence is a question.

links.note: 'Many such things did they say unto them, gnashing their teeth upon them, and spitting upon them, and saying, How shall we look when we are damned?' A five-word KJV singleton, and the singleton is the one place in the Bible where gnashing is an assault rather than a torment. With the stoning at 14:7, Ammonihah's treatment of the believers is Stephen's death distributed across the chapter.
links.text: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.

pericopes.text: And many such things, yea, all manner of such things did they say unto them; and thus they did mock them, for many days. And they did withhold food from them, that they might hunger, and water, that they might thirst; and they also did take from them their clothes, that they were naked; and thus they were bound with strong cords, and confined in prison.

provenance.other: “hunger and thirst and are naked” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:11 — 'Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace.' “are naked” occurs in exactly two, that verse and Hebrews 4:13, where the sense is 'laid open'. Alma 14:22 has all three of Paul's terms in Paul's order: 'they did withhold food from them, that they might HUNGER, and water, that they might THIRST; and they also did take from them their clothes, that they were NAKED'.
provenance.significance: Paul's triad is a list of what happens to apostles, and its point is that the Corinthians are full while the apostles starve. Alma 14:22 converts each item from a condition into a deliberate act, and states the intention every time: not that they hungered, but that food was withheld SO THAT they might hunger. The same three deprivations, three times attributed to a will. Behind it stands 1 Kings 22:27, where Micaiah is to be fed 'bread of affliction and water of affliction' until the king returns in peace — the Old Testament scene the chapter has been tracking since the blow on the cheek at 14:14 — and Ammonihah improves on Ahab by withholding both.

links.note: 'They did withhold food from them, that they might hunger, and water, that they might thirst; and they also did take from them their clothes, that they were naked.' Paul's three-term list of apostolic destitution, in his order, from a KJV singleton, with each term turned into a purpose clause. The machine proposed Genesis 3:7 here on 'that they were naked', which is the wrong nakedness; the exclusion register carries it.
links.text: Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;

pericopes.text: And it came to pass after they had thus suffered for many days, (and it was on the twelfth day, in the tenth month, in the tenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi,) that the Chief Judge over the land of Ammonihah, and many of their teachers and their Lawyers, went in unto the prison where Alma and Amulek was bound with cords.

And the Chief Judge stood before them, and smote them again, and saith unto them, If ye have the power of God, deliver yourselves from these bands, and then we will believe that the Lord will destroy this people according to your words.

provenance.other: “and we will believe him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:42, the chief priests at the cross: 'He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.' “come down from the cross” occurs in exactly three (Matthew 27:40, 27:42, Mark 15:30). Alma 14:24 has the conditional, the demand for self-deliverance and the promise of belief in Matthew's order: 'If ye have the power of God, deliver yourselves from these bands, and then we will believe.'
provenance.significance: This is the taunt reproduced whole, and the Book of Mormon has made only the substitutions the situation forces: 'the power of God' for 'the King of Israel', 'deliver yourselves from these bands' for 'come down from the cross'. The prior verse of the taunt is present too — Alma 14:20's 'If ye have such great power, why do ye not deliver yourselves?' is Matthew 27:40's 'If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross', and 14:15's 'ye see that ye had not power to save these which had been cast into the fire' is 27:42's 'He saved others; himself he cannot save'. All three clauses of the crucifixion mockery are in this chapter, in order, spread over ten verses. And the mockers are answered: at 14:25-28 the power of God does arrive, the bands are loosed, and the men who demanded the sign are killed by it. Matthew's taunt is left unanswered on the cross; Alma 14 answers it, which is a reading of Matthew 27:42 as much as a borrowing from it.

links.note: 'If ye have the power of God, deliver yourselves from these bands, and then we will believe that the Lord will destroy this people according to your words.' A five-word KJV singleton with the whole shape of the crucifixion mockery around it, and the chapter has already used the taunt's other two clauses at 14:15 and 14:20. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his thirty-six.
links.text: He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.

provenance.other: “the LORD will destroy this” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 19:14: 'Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.' Alma 14:24's clause is 'the Lord will destroy this people according to your words', and the words are put in the mouth of a man who is mocking.
provenance.significance: Genesis 19:14 is the KJV's one verse in which a warning of destruction is delivered and TAKEN AS A JOKE, and the Book of Mormon has kept both halves. Lot's sons-in-law think he is mocking; the chief judge of Ammonihah mocks the warning back at the men who gave it, in the same five words. What follows in each case is the same: Sodom is destroyed by fire and Ammonihah is destroyed in Alma 16:9-10, and this chapter has been full of fire since 14:8. The chief judge is telling a prophet what a prophet's warning sounds like to a man who does not believe it, and the sentence he uses to do it is the sentence a man used who was about to be burned.

links.note: 'And then we will believe that the Lord will destroy this people according to your words.' A five-word KJV singleton whose one occurrence is a destruction-warning that its hearers found funny. Held at moderate because the phrase is so natural a way to report a prophet's threat that the coincidence could be accidental — but the coincidence includes the mockery and the fire, and the city is destroyed two chapters later.
links.whyNot: Five ordinary words in an unremarkable order, and 'the Lord will destroy this people' is the substance of every prophetic warning in the book. The situational match with Genesis 19:14 is what carries the row, and a reader who reads it as coincidence has a fair case.
links.text: And Lot went out, and spake unto his sons in law, which married his daughters, and said, Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they all went forth and smote them, saying the same words, even until the last; and when the last had spoken unto them, the power of God was upon Alma and Amulek, and they arose and stood upon their feet;

provenance.other: “stood upon their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 11:11 — 'the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them.' The nearest relative is Ezekiel 37:10, 'and they lived, and stood up upon their feet', which has the extra preposition. “great fear” occurs in six KJV verses, and Revelation 11:11 is the one that joins it to men standing on their feet. Alma 14:25 reads 'the power of God was upon Alma and Amulek, and they arose and stood upon their feet', and Alma 14:29 reads 'they were struck with great fear'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 11 is the vision of the two witnesses, and Alma 14:25-29 follows it clause by clause. Two prophets who have prophesied against a city are overpowered by it; the city rejoices over them and torments them; then the spirit of life from God enters them and they stand upon their feet, and great fear falls on those who see; and 'the same hour was there a great earthquake, and the tenth part of the city FELL, and in the earthquake were slain of men seven thousand: and the remnant were affrighted' (11:13). The Book of Mormon has two prophets, a mocking city, a rising to the feet under the power of God, an earthquake, a building that falls, everyone inside it slain, and a remnant that runs. What Revelation gives as apocalyptic vision, Alma 14 gives as event — and the two witnesses of Revelation 11 are the only pair of prophets in the KJV to whom this happens, which is why the chapter's two-man ministry matters to the reading. The single word that anchors it is 'their': Revelation's witnesses are two, and its verbs are plural.

links.note: 'When the last had spoken unto them, the power of God was upon Alma and Amulek, and they arose and stood upon their feet.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the singleton belongs to the only passage in the Bible where two prophets, killed or overpowered by a hostile city, rise to their feet and are followed by an earthquake that drops a building and kills the onlookers. The sequence runs on through 14:27-29 and the recurrence list carries it. Ezekiel 37:10 is recorded as the alternative for the standing itself; it has no city, no pair, and no earthquake.
links.text: And after three days and an half the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them.

pericopes.text: and Alma cried, saying, How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength according to our faith which is in Christ, even unto deliverance; and they break the cords with which they were bound; and when the people saw this, they began to flee, for the fear of destruction had come upon them.

provenance.other: “How long, O Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 6:10. The psalter's versions are worded otherwise — Psalm 13:1 'How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?', Psalm 35:17 'Lord, how long wilt thou look on?', Habakkuk 1:2 'O LORD, how long shall I cry' — so the vocative in exactly this position is the Apocalypse's. Alma 14:26 reads 'How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 6:9-10 is the cry of 'the souls of them that were slain for the word of God … and they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?' Alma has just watched people burned for the word of God and has told Amulek, at 14:11, that their blood will 'cry mightily against them at the last day' — which is Revelation 6:10's petition in Alma's own words. Fifteen verses later he cries the martyrs' cry himself, in Revelation's exact vocative. The chapter has therefore quoted the same passage twice: once as a prediction about the dead and once as a prayer by the living, and the second is the first coming true early. Alma is granted what the souls under the altar are told to wait for.

links.note: 'And Alma cried, saying, How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength according to our faith which is in Christ, even unto deliverance.' Four words of a KJV singleton, and the singleton is the cry of martyrs killed for the word of God — which is precisely who has just died in this chapter, and precisely the reading Alma gave of their blood at 14:11.
links.text: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that so great was their fear, that they fell to the earth, and did not obtain the outer door of the prison; and the earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain, so that they fell to the earth; and the Chief Judge, and the Lawyers, and Priests, and teachers which smote upon Alma and Amulek, were slain by the fall thereof.

provenance.other: Two KJV singletons stand in one verse of Acts. “the foundations of the prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “bands were loosed” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, Acts 16:26 — 'And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.' Alma 14:27 has 'the earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain', and 14:28 has 'they were loosed from their bands'.
provenance.significance: Acts 16 is the New Testament's prison-earthquake and the Book of Mormon has taken the whole episode, not the sentence. Two missionaries are seized by a mob for interfering with the town's business, their clothes are torn off them (16:22, 'they rent off their clothes' — compare Alma 14:22, 'they also did take from them their clothes'), they are beaten, they are put in the inner prison, they pray, an earthquake shakes the prison's foundations, and every bond is loosed; the jailer 'came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas' (16:29), as the men of Ammonihah 'fell to the earth' at 14:27. The one change is the outcome, and it is total: in Acts the prison stands, nobody dies, and the jailer is converted; in Alma 14 the prison falls on the men inside it and every soul but the two prisoners is killed. Ammonihah gets Philippi's earthquake without Philippi's mercy, and the chapter has been arguing since 14:11 that this is just.

links.note: 'The earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain, so that they fell to the earth; and the Chief Judge, and the Lawyers, and Priests, and teachers which smote upon Alma and Amulek, were slain by the fall thereof.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of Acts 16 are distributed across Alma 14:27-28, and the surrounding episode matches at five further points set out in provenance. The 1830 spelling 'wrent' is the first edition's throughout.
links.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the temple veil at the death of Jesus. Matthew's is the one that continues 'and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent', so Matthew 27:51 alone joins a rending in twain to an earthquake — which is the pair Alma 14:27 has: 'the earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain'. The 1830 reads 'wrent', an archaic past participle the later editions kept.
provenance.significance: The chapter has been running the passion narrative since 14:14 — the blows on the cheek, the silence before the judge, Pilate's claim of power, the mockers' 'we will believe him' — and this is where it ends, on the two things Matthew reports at the moment of death. What is rent in Matthew is the veil that shut men out of the holy place; what is rent here is the wall that shut two prophets in. The reversal is exact and the Book of Mormon does not comment on it.

links.note: 'The walls of the prison were wrent in twain.' One of two KJV verses, and the one of the two that also has the earthquake Alma 14:27 supplies in the same clause. Held at moderate: three words, and the phrase is available English for anything torn in half. The Acts 16:26 row at this verse carries the stronger case and this one sits beside it as the passion chapter's closing echo.
links.whyNot: Three words, and the sense in Matthew is a curtain torn from top to bottom by God at the moment of death, not a wall thrown down by an earthquake. If the passion sequence across 14:14-24 is declined, this falls with it.
links.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;

pericopes.text: And Alma and Amulek came forth out of the prison, and they were not hurt; for the Lord had granted unto them power, according to their faith which was in Christ. And they straightway came forth out of the prison; and they were loosed from their bands; and the prison had fallen to the earth, and every soul which was within the walls thereof, save it were Alma and Amulek, were slain; and they straightway came forth into the city.

Now the people having heard a great noise, came running together by multitudes, to know the cause of it; and when they saw Alma and Amulek coming forth out of the prison, and the walls thereof had fallen to the earth, they were struck with great fear, and fled from the presence of Alma and Amulek, even as a goat fleeth with her young from two lions; and thus they did flee from the presence of Alma and Amulek.

And it came to pass that Alma and Amulek were commanded to depart out of that city; and they departed, and came out even into the land of Sidom; and behold, there they found all the people which had departed out of the land of Ammonihah, who had been cast out and stoned, because they believed in the words of Alma.
And they related unto them all that had happened unto their wives and children, and also concerning themselves, and of their power of deliverance.

And also Zeezrom lay sick at Sidom, with a burning fever, which was caused by the great tribulations of his mind, on account of his wickedness, for he supposed that Alma and Amulek was no more; and he supposed that they had been slain, by the cause of his iniquity. And this great sin, and his many other sins, did harrow up his mind until it did become exceeding sore, having no deliverance; therefore he began to be scorched with a burning heat.

provenance.other: “scorched” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 13:6 and Mark 4:6, of seed withering in the sun, and Revelation 16:9, 'and men were scorched with great heat'. Only the last has a person as its object. The adjective is from elsewhere: “burning heat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 32:24 and James 1:11, and neither uses the verb. Alma 15:3's 'he began to be scorched with a burning heat' is the Revelation construction with the other phrase's adjective. The passage's other half surfaces twelve verses later: “and they repented not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:9, and “repented not of their” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 16:11, and Alma 15:15 reads 'they repented not of their sins'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 16:8-11 is one movement — the fourth and fifth vials, men scorched with great heat, and twice over the refrain that they blasphemed and repented not — and Alma 15 has split it between two men and reversed the outcome for one of them. Zeezrom is scorched, and his scorching is explicitly not a plague but a conscience: 'a burning fever, which was caused by the great tribulations of his mind, on account of his wickedness.' He repents, and is healed. Ammonihah is not scorched at all, and at 15:15 'they repented not of their sins' in Revelation's own words — and Ammonihah is destroyed by fire in the next chapter. The vial's two halves have been distributed to the man who escapes it and the city that does not.

links.note: 'This great sin, and his many other sins, did harrow up his mind until it did become exceeding sore, having no deliverance; therefore he began to be scorched with a burning heat.' The verb is Revelation's and the adjective is James's; the clause that completes Revelation 16:9 arrives at 15:15 in the mouth of the narrator, about the city. Held at moderate — the individual phrases are short — but the two halves of the borrowing land twelve verses apart on the two parties the chapter is contrasting, which is more than a coincidence of vocabulary.
links.text: And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory.

pericopes.text: Now when he heard that Alma and Amulek was in the land of Sidom, his heart began to take courage; and he sent a message immediately unto them, desiring them to come unto him.

And it came to pass that they went immediately, obeying the message which he had sent unto them; and they went in unto the house unto Zeezrom; and they found him upon his bed sick, being very low with a burning fever; and his mind also was exceeding sore, because of his iniquities; and when he saw them, he stretched forth his hand, and besought them that they would heal him.
And it came to pass that Alma said unto him, taking him by the hand, Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?

provenance.other: Two KJV singletons frame the dialogue. “Believe ye that I am able” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 9:28; “according to your faith” occurs in exactly one, Matthew 9:29. Alma 15:5-10 runs the same four stages in the same order: the healers go IN UNTO THE HOUSE (Matthew 9:28, 'when he was come into the house'), the question is put — 'Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?' against 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?' — the answer is the same monosyllable, 'Yea' (Matthew 9:28, 'They said unto him, Yea, Lord'), and the healing is granted on the measure of the belief: 'heal him ACCORDING TO HIS FAITH which is in Christ' against 'ACCORDING TO YOUR FAITH be it unto you.' The intervening exchange at 15:8 has a third singleton behind it: “if thou believest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:37, Philip to the Ethiopian — 'If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest' — which is the KJV's one conditional-belief formula, and it is followed immediately by a baptism, as Alma 15:8 is followed by Zeezrom's at 15:12.
provenance.significance: Matthew 9:27-31 is the KJV's only healing conducted as a catechism. Everywhere else Jesus heals and then tells the person their faith has made them whole; here alone he asks first, receives an answer, and heals to the measure of it — which is exactly the shape of Alma 15:5-11, and it is the shape a missionary narrative needs, because a question and an answer can be preached where a miracle cannot. The Book of Mormon has also changed the object of belief in a way worth naming: Matthew's blind men are asked whether they believe Jesus is ABLE, a question about power, and Zeezrom is asked whether he believes 'in the power of Christ UNTO SALVATION' and then 'in the redemption of Christ' — the question about power has become a question about doctrine, and the healing that answers it is a conversion. Acts 8:37 supplies the second half of that conversion: the KJV's one 'if thou believest', a baptismal formula, and a baptism follows in both.

links.note: 'And Alma said unto him, taking him by the hand, Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?' Two KJV singletons hold the two ends of this dialogue — the question at Matthew 9:28 and the measure of the healing at Matthew 9:29 — and the four stages between them run in Matthew's order, including the bare 'Yea' and the entry into the house at 15:5. A third singleton, Acts 8:37's 'If thou believest', stands behind 15:8 and is followed in both texts by a baptism. Catalogued at 15:6 as the point where the question is asked; the recurrence list carries the rest of the scene.
links.text: And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.

provenance.other: “took her by the hand” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 9:25, Mark 1:31 and Luke 8:54 — and two of the three are the same raising of Jairus's daughter. Mark 1:31 is the odd one out, and it is the one whose patient has a FEVER: 'Simon's wife's mother lay sick of a fever … and he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her.' Alma 15:5 has Zeezrom 'upon his bed sick, being very low with a burning fever', and 15:6 has Alma 'taking him by the hand'.
provenance.significance: Of the KJV's hand-taking healings, only one is of a fever, and this chapter's patient has a fever — a fever, moreover, that the Book of Mormon has just explained psychosomatically, 'caused by the great tribulations of his mind, on account of his wickedness' (15:3). Mark 1:31 ends with the healed woman rising and ministering to the household; Alma 15:12 ends with Zeezrom baptized and beginning 'from that time forth to preach unto the people'. The pattern of immediate service after a fever is lifted is the same, and it is the only one of the three hand-takings that offers it.

links.note: 'Alma said unto him, taking him by the hand.' Four words shared with a three-verse phrase, and the choice among the three is made by the fever. Held at moderate: taking a sick man by the hand is what one does, and the gesture would need no source. It is written because Mark 1:31 is the single KJV verse in which that gesture cures a fever, and this is a fever.
links.whyNot: Four words, and the gesture is universal. Two of the three KJV verses containing the phrase are the same story, so 'exactly three' overstates the discrimination; and Acts 3:7's 'took him by the right hand', catalogued at 15:11, is a competing source for the same gesture in the same chapter.
links.text: And he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them.

pericopes.text: And he answered and said, Yea, I belive all the words that thou hast taught.
And Alma saith, If thou believest in the redemption of Christ, thou canst be healed.
And he saith, Yea, I believe according to thy words.
And then Alma cried unto the Lord, saying, O Lord our God, have mercy on this man, and heal him according to his faith which is in Christ.

And it came to pass that when Alma had said these words, that Zeezrom leaped upon his feet, and began to walk; and this was done to the great astonishment of all the people; and the knowledge of this went forth throughout all the land of Sidom.

provenance.other: “leaping up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:8, and the whole clause “and he leaping up stood and walked” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. The gesture that precedes it is also absolute: “took him by the right hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:7. Alma 15:6 has 'taking him by the hand' and 15:11 has 'Zeezrom leaped upon his feet, and began to walk'.
provenance.significance: Acts 3 is the New Testament's model apostolic healing — two missionaries, a man who cannot rise, a hand taken, a leap, walking, and a crowd — and Alma 15:5-11 has all six with two missionaries of its own. What the Book of Mormon changes is the public sequel. In Acts the crowd 'ran together unto them … greatly wondering' (3:11) and Peter turns the wonder into a sermon; in Alma 15:11 the healing 'was done to the great astonishment of all the people; and the knowledge of this went forth throughout all the land of Sidom', and the sermon is preached at 15:12 by the healed man himself. Zeezrom, the lawyer who at Alma 11 was paid to trap Alma with words, is the one who begins to preach — which is the chapter's real point and is why the healing had to be public.

links.note: 'Zeezrom leaped upon his feet, and began to walk; and this was done to the great astonishment of all the people.' Two KJV singletons stand in the two verses of Acts 3 that this scene reproduces, and their gestures are distributed exactly as Acts distributes them: the hand at Alma 15:6 as at Acts 3:7, the leaping and walking at Alma 15:11 as at Acts 3:8, and the astonished crowd at Alma 15:11 as at Acts 3:10-11. No clause is reproduced verbatim, which is why this is an allusion; the sequence is what carries it.
links.text: And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.

pericopes.text: And Alma baptized Zeezrom unto the Lord; and he began from that time forth to preach unto the people.
And Alma established a Church in the land of Sidom, and consecrated Priests and teachers in the land, to baptize unto the Lord whosoever were desirous to be baptized.
And it came to pass that they were many; for they did flock in from all the region round about Sidom, and were baptized;

provenance.other: “the region round about” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 3:5, Mark 1:28, Luke 4:14 and Luke 7:17. Three of the four are about a REPORT spreading outward from Jesus; only Matthew 3:5 is about PEOPLE coming inward, and only Matthew 3:5 is followed by a baptism — 'Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.' Alma 15:14 reads 'they did flock in from all the region round about Sidom, and were baptized.'
provenance.significance: The verse before this one has Alma establishing a church and consecrating priests 'to baptize unto the Lord whosoever were desirous to be baptized', and this one describes the response in the KJV's words for the response to John the Baptist. The place-name is put where Matthew puts Jordan — 'the region round about Sidom' for 'the region round about Jordan' — so the town takes the river's grammatical position. That is a small thing and it is the whole borrowing: what a mass baptism looks like, in the only English sentence the KJV offers for one.

links.note: 'For they did flock in from all the region round about Sidom, and were baptized.' One of four KJV verses, and the only one of the four that has people coming rather than a rumour going, and the only one followed by baptism. Moderate: four words, and 'the region round about' is available English — but the phrase arrives here attached to the same event it names in Matthew.
links.text: Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan,

pericopes.text: but as to the people that were in the land of Ammonihah, they yet remained a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people; and they repented not of their sins, ascribing all the power of Alma and Amulek to the Devil: for they were of the profession of Nehor, and did not believe in the repentance of their sins.

provenance.route: Ezekiel 3:7 with Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “hardhearted” as one word occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 3:7: 'all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.' Its partner is common — “stiffnecked” occurs in nine KJV verses, six of them Exodus and Deuteronomy on the golden calf, and the ninth is Acts 7:51, Stephen's 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost'. Alma 15:15 pairs the singleton with the common word: 'they yet remained a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people'. The verse's last clause is Revelation's — “repented not of their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:11 — and completes the borrowing begun at 15:3.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 3:7 is not a description but a warning issued to a prophet before he is sent: the house of Israel will not hearken to you, because they will not hearken to me, because they are impudent and hardhearted. Alma has just been sent to Ammonihah, has been rejected, imprisoned and delivered, and this verse is the narrator's verdict on the mission — the one KJV word for a people constitutionally unable to hear, applied to the one city in the Book of Mormon where preaching wholly fails. Stephen's 'ye stiffnecked … ye do always resist the Holy Ghost' supplies the other half, and its charge is the one Ammonihah is about to incur in the next clause, where the power of Alma and Amulek is ascribed to the devil.

links.note: 'They yet remained a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people; and they repented not of their sins.' The KJV's one occurrence of 'hardhearted' is Ezekiel's word for the audience a prophet is warned about before he goes, and the pairing with 'stiffnecked' is the Book of Mormon's own. Moderate: the two words are separately available and their conjunction is not a KJV collocation.
links.text: But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared; the row is figural and is recorded as such. The KJV's charge is 'He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils' (Mark 3:22, with Matthew 12:24), and the Book of Mormon's is 'ascribing all the power of Alma and Amulek to the Devil'. The relevant fact about the KJV passage is what Jesus makes of the charge: Mark 3:29-30 turns it into the one unforgivable sin, 'he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness … BECAUSE THEY SAID, He hath an unclean spirit.'
provenance.significance: Alma 15:15 reports two things about Ammonihah in one sentence — that they ascribed the power to the devil, and that they 'did not believe in the repentance of their sins' — and in the KJV those two things are one thing. Mark 3:30 defines the unpardonable sin by exactly the accusation Ammonihah makes, and a sin that cannot be forgiven is a sin one cannot repent of. The city that at 14:7 asked Zeezrom 'Art thou also possessed with the Devil?' has, on the New Testament's own terms, put itself beyond the repentance it disbelieves in — and it is destroyed in the next chapter. The Book of Mormon never cites Mark 3; the sequence of the sentence does the work.

links.note: 'Ascribing all the power of Alma and Amulek to the Devil: for they were of the profession of Nehor, and did not believe in the repentance of their sins.' A figural link with no verbal contact, written because the two clauses of the verse stand in the same relation the KJV puts them in at Mark 3:22-30: attribute a divine power to the devil, and you have committed the sin that is not forgiven. Moderate, and the whyNot is real.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal whatever is shared, and attributing a rival's miracles to the devil is a commonplace of religious polemic that needs no source. The link is an argument about the logic of the verse, not about its wording, and a reader who wants dependence demonstrated will decline it.
links.text: And the scribes which came down from Jerusalem said, He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma and Amulek, Amulek having forsaken all his gold, and his silver, and his precious things, which was in the land of Ammonihah, for the word of God, he being rejected by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred;

provenance.other: “forsaken all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:27 — Peter's 'Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee'. The synoptic parallels use the other verb: Mark 10:28 and Luke 18:28 both read 'Lo, we have LEFT all'. Two verses later Matthew itemises what forsaking all means: 'every one that hath FORSAKEN houses, or brethren, or sisters, or FATHER, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake'. Alma 15:16 has Matthew's verb and Matthew's list, adapted: Amulek 'having forsaken all his gold, and his silver, and his precious things … for the word of God, he being rejected by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has separated what Matthew fuses, and the separation is the reading. In Matthew 19:29 the possessions and the relatives are one list of things a disciple gives up. In Alma 15:16 the property is forsaken — an act of Amulek's — and the family is lost, a thing done TO him: 'he being REJECTED by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred'. Matthew's disciple leaves his father; Amulek's father leaves him. Matthew promises the forsaker 'an hundredfold, and … everlasting life'; Alma 15:18 gives Amulek the smaller and more immediate compensation, which is a house — Alma 'took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations'. The chapter answers Peter's question, 'what shall we have therefore?', with hospitality.

links.note: 'Amulek having forsaken all his gold, and his silver, and his precious things … for the word of God, he being rejected by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred.' The verb is a KJV singleton and the synoptic control is clean: Mark and Luke read 'left all' where Matthew reads 'forsaken all', and the Book of Mormon has Matthew's. The itemised loss two verses later in Matthew supplies the father and the kindred.
links.text: And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.

pericopes.text: therefore, after Alma having established the Church at Sidom, seeing a great check, yea, seeing that the people were checked as to the pride of their hearts, and began to humble themselves before God, and began to assemble themselves together at their sanctuaries to worship God before the altar, watching and praying continually, that they might be delivered from Satan, and from death, and from destruction:

Now as I said, Alma having seen all these things, therefore he took Amulek and came over to the land of Zarahemla, and took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations, and strengthened him in the Lord.

provenance.other: “strengthened his hand in God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 23:16 — 'And Jonathan Saul's son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.' It is the KJV's only instance of one man strengthening another IN God; every other use of 'strengthened' in the Old Testament is of a king strengthening himself, or of God strengthening a man. Alma 15:18 reads 'he took Amulek and came over to the land of Zarahemla, and took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations, and strengthened him in the Lord.'
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one model for what Alma does in this verse, and it is a friendship under persecution: Jonathan goes to David in the wood while Saul is hunting him, and does nothing but strengthen his hand in God. Alma 15:18 is the same act performed for a man who has just lost his property, his friends and his family for the word of God, and the Book of Mormon's phrasing shifts the preposition from Jonathan's 'in God' to 'in the Lord' while keeping the construction. It is also the last sentence of the Ammonihah narrative, and it is domestic — after burning, imprisonment, earthquake and mass baptism, the chapter ends with one man taking another home.

links.note: 'He took Amulek and came over to the land of Zarahemla, and took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations, and strengthened him in the Lord.' A KJV singleton with one noun changed, and the singleton is the Bible's one scene of a friend strengthening a fugitive in God. Moderate rather than high: 'strengthened him in the Lord' is natural English and a writer could reach it without Jonathan in view, and no other element of 1 Samuel 23 is present.
links.whyNot: Four words, one of them altered, and the phrase is unremarkable devotional English. Nothing else of the Jonathan and David episode appears in Alma 15, and the argument rests on the rarity count plus a situational likeness.
links.text: And Jonathan Saul’s son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.

pericopes.text: And thus ended the tenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And it came to pass in the eleventh year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, on the fifth day of the second month, there having been much peace in the land of Zarahemla; there having been no wars nor contentions for a certain number of years; even until the fifth day of the second month, in the eleventh year, there was a cry of war heard throughout the land;
for behold, the armies of the Lamanites had come in on the wilderness side, into the borders of the land, even into the city of Ammonihah, and began to slay the people, and to destroy the city.

And now it came to pass before the Nephites could raise a sufficient army to drive them out of the land, they had destroyed the people which were in the city of Ammonihah, and also some around the borders of Noah, and taking others captive into the wilderness.
Now it came to pass that the Nephites were desirous to obtain those which had been carried away captive into the wilderness;

links.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the remnant of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to him, with the rest of the people that remained.

provenance.other: "carried away captive into" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Jeremiah 39:9. "carried away captive" without the preposition is formulaic — 22 KJV verses, most of them Jeremiah's — so the whole of the rarity sits in the four-word run that names a destination.
provenance.significance: The phrase is the one the book opened with. At 1 Nephi 1:13 Lehi foresees that many 'should be carried away captive into Babylon', reproducing the KJV's only instance of the phrase; here, at the far end of the corpus, the same singleton returns with 'the wilderness' where Jeremiah and Lehi had Babylon. What is done with it is the finding. Jeremiah 39 is a deportation nobody comes back from, executed by a captain of the guard; Alma 16 sends its own chief captain after the column, and 16:8 reports that 'there was not one soul of them which had been lost'. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one sentence for irreversible exile and writes the reversal of it.

links.note: 'Those which had been carried away captive into the wilderness.' A four-word KJV singleton, carried across a book boundary from 1 Nephi 1:13 where the argument for it was made, and used here in a new hand with the wilderness substituted for Babylon. The machine ranked Ezra 2:1 first on this verse ('those which had been carried away'), which is the same deportation seen from the return; Jeremiah 39:9 is the verse the wording actually reproduces.

pericopes.text: therefore he that had been appointed Chief Captain over the armies of the Nephites, (and his name was Zoram, and he had two sons, Lehi and Aha:) Now Zoram and his two sons, knowing that Alma was High Priest over the Church, and having heard that he had the spirit of prophecy, therefore they went unto him and desired of him to know whether the Lord would that they should go into the wilderness in search of their brethren, who had been taken captive by the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that Alma inquired of the Lord concerning the matter. And Alma returned and said unto them, Behold the Lamanites will cross the river Sidon in the south wilderness, away up beyond the borders of the land of Manti.—And behold there shall ye meet them, on the east of the river Sidon, and there the Lord will deliver unto thee thy brethren which have been taken captive by the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that Zoram and his sons crossed over the river Sidon, with their armies, and marched away beyond the borders of Manti, into the south wilderness, which was on the east side of the river Sidon.

And they came upon the armies of the Lamanites, and the Lamanites were scattered and driven into the wilderness; and they took their brethren which had been taken captive by the Lamanites, and there was not one soul of them which had been lost, that were taken captive. And they were brought by their brethren to possess their own lands.

And thus ended the eleventh year of the Judges, the Lamanites having been driven out of the land, and the people of Ammonihah were destroyed; yea, every living soul of the Ammonihahites were destroyed, and also their great city, which they said God could not destroy, because of its greatness.—
But behold, in one day it was left desolate; and their carcases were mangled by dogs and wild beasts of the wilderness;

links.text: And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the LORD: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy.

provenance.other: "the dogs to tear" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse and "beasts of the earth to devour" occurs in exactly 1, both Jeremiah 15:3. Only two KJV verses name dogs and beasts together — Exodus 22:31, where the dogs are fed carrion under a purity law, and Jeremiah 15:3, where dogs and 'the beasts of the earth' are two of four kinds appointed over a people to devour them. Jeremiah 15:3 is the Bible's only sentence in which dogs and wild beasts are executioners of a nation.
provenance.significance: Abinadi threatened Noah's people with this verse at Mosiah 12:2 — 'the vultures of the air, and the dogs, yea, and the wild beasts, shall devour their flesh' — and the threat was not carried out in that generation. Here the same scavengers are reported as fact over the corpses of Ammonihah, in narration rather than prophecy, without the prophet who spoke them being anywhere in the chapter. The book has moved a Jeremiah oracle from the mouth of a condemned preacher into the record of what happened, which is what Jeremiah 15 itself does: verse 1 refuses intercession, verse 3 appoints the four kinds, and Ammonihah is the city that had already voted its two intercessors out of it.

links.note: 'Their carcases were mangled by dogs and wild beasts of the wilderness.' The link was argued at Mosiah 12:2 and is written again here because Alma is a new book and a new voice — see ADJUDICATING §4. Two things separate this occurrence from that one: it is narrative rather than oracle, and it drops Jeremiah's birds. The 1830 'their carcases', changed to 'the carcases' in 1920, keeps the possessive that ties the corpses to the boasting Ammonihahites of the previous verse.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, after many days, their dead bodies were heaped up upon the face of the earth, and they were covered with a shallow covering. And now so great was the scent thereof, that the people did not go in to possess the land of Ammonihah for many years. And it was called desolation of Nehors; for they were of the profession of Nehor, which were slain; and their lands remained desolate.

links.text: They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth: and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.

provenance.other: 'Upon the face of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest formulas and proves nothing by itself; what is shared with Jeremiah 16:4 is the compound — bodies unburied, lying on the face of the earth, and left to carcase-eating animals — which the KJV assembles in this verse and, in a shorter form, at Psalm 79:2 and Jeremiah 34:20.
provenance.significance: Read with 16:10 this is two consecutive Jeremiah chapters used for two consecutive Book of Mormon verses: 15:3 supplies the animals, 16:4 the unburied bodies on the open ground. Jeremiah 16:4's point is the withholding of burial as a judgment, and Alma 16:11's oddest detail answers it exactly — the corpses are eventually 'covered with a shallow covering', a burial that is not one, done not out of respect but because of the smell. The land is then left empty for years and renamed for the heresy of the men in it. Jeremiah's sentence is that the dead of Judah will be as dung on the face of the earth; the Book of Mormon carries it out and then names the field.

links.note: 'Their dead bodies were heaped up upon the face of the earth, and they were covered with a shallow covering.' Catalogued at moderate: the verbal contact is a compound of ordinary phrases rather than a rare string, and it is the combination — unburied, on the face of the earth, eaten by animals, in a land afterwards uninhabitable — that points at Jeremiah 16:4 and at the chapter before it. 'Shallow' occurs in no KJV verse at all, which is a small sign that the sentence is being composed rather than quoted.
links.whyNot: No run of shared words here exceeds the Book of Mormon's own boilerplate. A reader who declines the link is declining a cumulative case, not a verbal one, and that is a defensible thing to decline.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did not come again to war against the Nephites until the fourteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi. And thus for three years did the people of Nephi have continual peace in all the land.
And Alma and Amulek went forth preaching repentance unto the people in their tempels, and in their sanctuaries, and also in their synagogues, which was built after the manner of the Jews.

links.text: Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.

provenance.other: "manner of the Jews" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 19:40. The Book of Mormon uses it four times — 2 Nephi 25:2 and 25:6, Alma 11:4 ('the manner of the Jews' reckoning'), and here.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one phrase for a Jewish custom named as such, and it is a burial rite performed on the body of Jesus. The Book of Mormon adopts that phrase as its standing formula for everything Jewish it wants to hold at arm's length — Nephi's refusal to teach his children after it, the Nephite system of weights, and here the architecture of the synagogues. Whether the borrowing is deliberate or the phrase is simply the one available to a writer whose English is the KJV's, the effect is the same: the Book of Mormon's word for Jewishness comes from the one verse where a Jewish custom is done for Christ.

links.note: 'Their synagogues, which was built after the manner of the Jews.' A KJV singleton put to a use the KJV never puts it to — John's is a burial, Alma's is a building. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion for that reason, and at moderate rather than high because the construction 'after the manner of X' is common English and the Book of Mormon may simply be filling a slot. Its interest is that the slot has exactly one KJV filler. The 1830 'which was built' for a plural subject, corrected to 'which were built' in 1920, is the first edition's grammar and carries nothing here.
links.whyNot: Four uses across three books look more like a house formula than a live allusion, and the sense is not John's. A reader may reasonably file this under the Index Verborum rather than as a link.

pericopes.text: And as many as would hear their words, unto them they did impart the word of God, without any respects of persons continually.

And thus did Alma and Amulek go forth, and also many more which had been chosen for the work, to preach the word throughout all the land. And the establishment of the Church became general throughout the land, in all the region round about, among all the people of the Nephites.

And there was no inequality among them, for the Lord did pour out his spirit on all the face of the land, for to prepare the minds of the children of men, or to prepare their hearts to recieve the word which should be taught among them at the time of his coming,

links.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

provenance.mt: Joel 2:28 — 'I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh'.
provenance.route: Joel 2:28 → KJV → Book of Mormon, NOT via Acts 2:17
provenance.other: "pour out my spirit upon" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Joel 2:28. Acts 2:17 quotes the same oracle with a partitive — 'I will pour out OF my Spirit upon all flesh' — and Alma 16:16 has no partitive: 'the Lord did pour out his spirit on all the face of the land'. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence on this pair, exactly as it did at Mosiah 25:24, because the divergence is a single common word and the tool suppresses those by design.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Joel and Acts both pour the spirit 'upon all flesh'; Alma pours it 'on all the face of the land'. The universal object of the prophecy has been exchanged for a territory, and the effect named is not prophecy, dreams or visions but the abolition of inequality and the preparing of minds to receive a word 'at the time of his coming'. Joel's Pentecost is turned into a demographic condition of a country, and the outpouring becomes preparatory rather than climactic — the spirit is poured out so that a later preaching can land.

links.note: 'The Lord did pour out his spirit on all the face of the land.' Joel's clause in the third person and without Peter's partitive, which is what settles the mediation as direct-OT; the argument was made in full at Mosiah 25:24 and is not repeated. 'On all the face of' is a Book of Mormon formula occurring in twenty-nine verses of the 1830 text and is not evidence for Acts 17:26, where it is a KJV singleton — see the exclusion at this verse.

pericopes.text: that they might not be hardened against the word, that they might not be unbelieving, and go on to destruction, but that they might recieve the word with joy, and as a branch be grafted into the true vine, that they might enter into the rest of the Lord their God.

links.text: They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.

provenance.other: "receive the word with joy" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Luke 8:13. "true vine" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 15:1. The KJV never spells the grafting word 'grafted'; Romans 11 has 'graffed' at 11:17, 11:19, 11:23 and 11:24, so the image is Paul's and the orthography is the Book of Mormon's own.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best sentence and the two singletons are doing opposite work. Luke 8:13's hearers on the rock 'receive the word with joy' and the next clause is 'and these have no root' — in the parable of the sower that phrase is the mark of the hearer who does not last. Alma 16:17 takes the phrase and immediately supplies what Luke's hearers lacked: 'that they might receive the word with joy, and as a branch be grafted into the true vine'. Grafting is the one operation that gives a branch a root it did not grow. So the verse quotes the KJV's definition of rootless joy and then cures it, by fusing Paul's olive-tree graft with John's vine — and the vine John 15 goes on to describe is the one whose branches are pruned or burned according to whether they abide. Neither Luke, nor Paul, nor John says this. The composite says it.

links.note: 'That they might receive the word with joy, and as a branch be grafted into the true vine, that they might enter into the rest of the Lord their God.' Three New Testament images in fourteen words, two of them KJV singletons. The final clause, 'enter into the rest of the Lord their God', is the Book of Mormon's own settled phrase and is adjudicated where Alma's argument for it is made, in chapters 12-13; its Psalm 95 / Hebrews 3 mediation was decided at Jacob 1:7. Filed here as an exclusion pointing there rather than as a fourth source on this row.

pericopes.text: Now those priests which did go forth among the people, did preach against all lyings, and deceivings, and envyings, and strifes, and malice, and revilings, and stealing, robbing, plundering, murdering, committing adultery, and all manner of lasciviousness, crying that these things ought not so to be;

links.text: Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.

provenance.other: "these things ought not so to be" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, James 3:10. Seven consecutive words, well below Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold for a long KJV quotation, so this is not one of his thirty-six and should not be read as one.
provenance.significance: Recover James 3 and the borrowing turns out to have selected its list. James 3 is the chapter on the tongue — the bit and the bridle, the rudder, the fire, the untameable member, blessing and cursing out of the same mouth — and its verdict on all of it is the sentence Alma's priests are given. The Book of Mormon's list opens with six sins of speech in a row: lyings, deceivings, envyings, strifes, malice, revilings. Only then does it move to theft, robbery, plunder, murder, adultery. The KJV sentence about the mouth is attached to a catalogue whose first half is the mouth, and the preachers are said to be 'crying' it — using the member the source verse condemns.

links.note: 'Crying that these things ought not so to be.' A seven-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly, which the n-gram stream ranked first on this verse at rarity 4.00 — one of the rare occasions in this project where the machine found the chapter's plainest quotation on its own. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length, per CONVENTIONS §2. James's vocative 'My brethren' is dropped, which is what converts an apostolic address into a summary of what preachers said.

pericopes.text: holding forth things which must shortly come; yea, holding forth the coming of the Son of God, his sufferings and death, and also the resurrection of the dead.

links.text: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:

provenance.route: Revelation 1:1 + Philippians 2:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "things which must shortly come to pass" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 1:1, and the shorter "shortly come to pass" occurs in exactly 1 as well. "holding forth" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Philippians 2:16 — 'Holding forth the word of life'. The 1830 text reads 'things which must shortly come', without Revelation's 'to pass'; the 1920 and current editions read the same, so this is not a case where a later edition moved the text toward the source.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons fused in nine words, and the fusion is exact about what preaching is. Philippians 2:16 supplies the verb — Paul's converts hold forth 'the word of life' in the midst of a crooked generation — and Revelation 1:1 supplies the object, the things that must shortly come to pass, which in Revelation are what an angel shows John. Alma's priests do both: they hold forth, as Paul's Philippians do, the thing an apocalypse discloses. The content the verse then names is not apocalyptic at all but the coming, sufferings, death and resurrection of the Son of God — so the frame of the seer's book has been put around the content of the gospel.

links.note: 'Holding forth things which must shortly come; yea, holding forth the coming of the Son of God, his sufferings and death, and also the resurrection of the dead.' The doubled participle carries a singleton on each side of it. Revelation 1:1 is the sole KJV home of the phrase and Philippians 2:16 the sole home of the verb, and neither is a phrase the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere. The closing 'the resurrection of the dead' is a New Testament commonplace in eleven KJV verses and is not evidence for 1 Corinthians 15:21, which the machine ranked here.

pericopes.text: And many of the people did inquire concerning the place where the Son of God should come; and they were taught that he would appear unto them after his resurrection; and this the people did hear with great joy and gladness.

And now after the Church having been established throughout all the land, having got the victory over the Devil, and the word of God being preached in its purity in all the land; and the Lord pouring out his blessings upon the people; and thus ended the fourteenth year of the reign of the Judges, over the people of Nephi.

links.text: And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.

provenance.other: "the victory over" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 15:2. The construction is not otherwise available in the King James Bible: 1 Corinthians 15:57 has 'giveth us the victory' with no object, and Mosiah 15:8's 'gained the victory over death' is that verse crossed with this one. The Book of Mormon reads 'having got the victory over the Devil' where Revelation has 'had gotten the victory over the beast'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 15:2 and 15:3 are used at the two ends of this corpus. The pilot's flagship row is 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi's praise reproduces six words of Revelation 15:3 — the song of Moses and of the Lamb — sung, in Revelation, by exactly the people described one verse earlier as having gotten the victory over the beast. Alma 16:21 takes that earlier verse. And it makes the substitution Revelation itself licenses: the beast's authority comes from the dragon, 'that old serpent, called the Devil' at Revelation 12:9, so 'the victory over the Devil' names the power behind the figure John's conquerors defeat. A church established throughout the land, with the word preached in its purity, is being described in the vocabulary of the martyrs standing on the sea of glass.

links.note: 'And now after the Church having been established throughout all the land, having got the victory over the Devil.' Four words of a KJV singleton, with 'got' for 'gotten' and the Devil for the beast. No edition corrects 'got' to Revelation's 'gotten' — 1920 and the current text keep 'having got the victory over the devil' and change only the surrounding clause ('the Church having been established' → 'the church had been established'), so the departure from the source at this word is the Book of Mormon's throughout its printed history. This is a chapter-closing summary, not a vision, and the borrowing is what gives an administrative sentence its eschatological register.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that as Alma was journeying from the land of Gideon, southward, away to the land of Manti, behold, to his astonishment, he met with the sons of Mosiah, a journeying towards the land of Zarahemla.

Now these sons of Mosiah were with Alma at the time the angel first appeared unto him; therefore Alma did rejoice exceedingly, to see his brethren; and what added more to his joy, they were still his brethren in the Lord; yea, and they had waxed strong in the knowledge of the truth; for they were men of a sound understanding, and they had searched the Scriptures diligently, that they might know the word of God.

links.text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

provenance.other: "searched the scriptures" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 17:11. The imperative "search the scriptures" occurs in exactly 1, John 5:39. Alma 17:2 has the past tense — 'they had searched the Scriptures diligently' — which is Acts 17:11's inflection and not John's.
provenance.alternative: John 5:39, 'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life', which is the better-known verse and the one a modern reader hears first. It is the wrong grammar: John has a command and Alma a completed action, and Acts supplies both the tense and the adverb slot.
provenance.significance: Acts 17:11 is the KJV's one commendation of scripture-searching, and it commends the Bereans for searching in order to test what two visiting missionaries were preaching. Alma 17:2 gives the same praise to men who searched in order to become the missionaries. The one substitution is the adverb: Luke's Bereans searched 'daily', the sons of Mosiah 'diligently' — frequency exchanged for thoroughness, which is the difference between a congregation checking a sermon and a preacher preparing one. The Book of Mormon has taken the Bible's model hearers and made them its model senders.

links.note: 'They had waxed strong in the knowledge of the truth; for they were men of a sound understanding, and they had searched the Scriptures diligently.' The verse is built out of New Testament phrases that are individually unremarkable and jointly Lukan and Pauline: 'waxed strong' occurs in two KJV verses, both Luke's of a growing child (1:80, 2:40); 'knowledge of the truth' in three, all in the Pastorals and Hebrews; and 'searched the scriptures' in one. The machine ranked 2 Timothy 3:7 here on 'the knowledge of the truth', which is a genuine Pastoral formula but the least distinctive thing in the sentence.

pericopes.text: But this is not all: they had given themselves to much prayer, and fasting, therefore they had the spirit of prophecy, and the spirit of revelation, and when they taught, they taught with power and authority, even as with the power and authority of God.

links.text: Then he called his twelve disciples together, and gave them power and authority over all devils, and to cure diseases.

provenance.other: "power and authority" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, both in Luke: 9:1, where Jesus gives the twelve power and authority and sends them out, and 20:20, where spies try to deliver him up to the power and authority of the governor. The n-gram stream ranked 20:20 first here because its six-word run is longer; 9:1 is the verse whose situation Alma 17:3 reproduces.
provenance.significance: The 1830 text says the sons of Mosiah 'taught with power and authority, even as with the power and authority of God' — the phrase twice, the second time referred to its origin. In Luke 9:1 power and authority are precisely a delegation: the twelve have them because they were given them for a journey they are about to take. Alma 17 is that journey's Book of Mormon equivalent, and the chapter goes on to use Luke 9's sending elsewhere — the arms carried in to Lamoni at 17:39 are brought 'for a testimony', which is what Luke 9:5's disciples leave behind them. The 1920 edition deleted the second half of the doubling, and with it the clause that made the delegation explicit.

links.note: 'And when they taught, they taught with power and authority, even as with the power and authority of God.' A two-verse KJV phrase used in the sense of the one of the two that is about missionaries. Catalogued at moderate because 'power and authority' is a natural English pair and the Book of Mormon may have arrived at it independently; what argues for Luke 9:1 is that both texts have the phrase as something conferred for a mission. The 1830 doubling, deleted in 1920, is the first edition preserving the argument the modern text only implies.

pericopes.text: And they had been teaching the word of God for the space of fourteen years, among the Lamanites, having had much success in bringing many to the knowledge of the truth; yea, by the power of their words, many were brought before the altar of God, to call on his name, and confess their sins before him.

Now these are the circumstances which attended them in their journeyings, for they had many afflictions; they did suffer much, both in body and in mind; such as hunger, thirst and fatigue, and also much labor in the spirit.

links.text: In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.

provenance.other: "in hunger and thirst" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:27. "journeyings" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Numbers 10:28 and 2 Corinthians 11:26 — and 11:26 is the verse immediately before. So the two rare words in Alma 17:5 come from two consecutive verses of one passage, in that passage's order.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 11 is the peristasis catalogue, Paul's list of what he has suffered, offered as credentials against rival apostles and framed by him as foolish boasting. Alma 17:5 is doing exactly that work at exactly that point: the narrator has just claimed at 17:3-4 that these men had the spirit of prophecy and fourteen years' success, and the hardship list is what makes the claim credible rather than boastful. The Book of Mormon has borrowed the New Testament's one apostolic résumé and put it in the third person, which removes the embarrassment Paul spends the whole chapter apologising for. And 11:26's 'perils of robbers' sits three lines from Alma's own account of a people who lived by robbing and plundering.

links.note: 'Now these are the circumstances which attended them in their journeyings, for they had many afflictions; they did suffer much, both in body and in mind; such as hunger, thirst and fatigue.' A KJV singleton and a two-verse KJV word, taken from consecutive verses. The machine offered 1 Corinthians 7:34 on 'both in body and', which is the married-and-unmarried discussion and has nothing to do with hardship; the run is real and the sense is not. The same two words return at Alma 18:37, where Ammon rehearses to Lamoni 'all the journeyings of their fathers in the wilderness, and all their sufferings with hunger and thirst' — the pair reused within the same book for Lehi's company rather than the missionaries', and recorded there as a recurrence rather than a fresh borrowing.

pericopes.text: Now these were their journeyings, having taken leave of their father Mosiah, in the first year of the reign of the Judges; having refused the kingdom which their father was desirous to confer upon them; and also this was the minds of the people;

nevertheless they departed out of the land of Zarahemla, and took their swords, and their spears, and their bows, and their arrows, and their slings; and this they done that they might provide food for themselves while in the wilderness:

links.text: And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.

provenance.other: "slings" in the plural occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 26:14, which is also the KJV's only inventory of an army's equipment ending in slings. Alma 17:7 lists swords, spears, bows, arrows and slings; the three items the two lists share — spears, bows, slings — stand in the same order in both.
provenance.significance: The one time the King James Bible equips a whole host with slings, it is Uzziah doing it, and the next thing the chapter records is that his heart was lifted up to his destruction and he was struck with leprosy for taking a priest's office. Alma 17:6-7 has just said that the sons of Mosiah refused the kingdom their father wished to confer on them, and then arms itself out of the king's armoury — and takes the weapons, the verse insists, only to hunt food. The chapter ends with one of them using the sling anyway. Whether the writer saw the Uzziah frame or not, the Book of Mormon's princes are given a king's equipment at precisely the verse where they decline to be kings.

links.note: 'They took their swords, and their spears, and their bows, and their arrows, and their slings; and this they done that they might provide food for themselves.' Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: a weapons list is the sort of thing two texts can compose alike, and the shared items are the obvious ones. What lifts it above coincidence is the plural 'slings', which the KJV uses once, and the order. The 1830's 'this they done' for 'this they did' is the first edition's grammar and bears nothing.
links.whyNot: Nothing here is quoted. A reader may fairly hold that the Book of Mormon is listing the weapons a wilderness party would carry and that the overlap with Uzziah's armoury is what any two such lists would share.

pericopes.text: and thus they departed into the wilderness, with their numbers which they had selected, to go up to the land of Nephi, to preach the word of God unto the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that they journeyed many days in the wilderness, and they fasted much, and prayed much, that the Lord would grant unto them a portion of his spirit to go with them, and abide with them, that they might be an instrument in the hands of God, to bring, if it were possible, their brethren, the Lamanites, to the knowledge of the truth; to the knowledge of the baseness of the traditions of their fathers, which were not correct.
And it came to pass that the Lord did visit them with his spirit, and said unto them, Be comforted; and they were comforted.

And the Lord said unto them also, Go forth among the Lamanites, thy brethren, and establish my word; yet ye shall be patient in long suffering and afflictions, that ye may shew forth good examples unto them in me, and I will make an instrument of thee in my hands, unto the salvation of many souls.

links.text: Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting.

provenance.other: "shew forth all longsuffering" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Timothy 1:16. Neither component is rare on its own — 'shew forth' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and 'longsuffering' in seventeen — and they meet in this verse alone. Alma 17:11 has both, in the same order, with the same governing purpose clause, and with the same prepositional phrase 'in me' attached: 'that ye may shew forth good examples unto them in me'.
provenance.significance: The structure is reproduced whole and the roles are exchanged. In 1 Timothy the longsuffering is Christ's, displayed in Paul, so that Paul becomes 'a pattern to them which should hereafter believe'; in Alma the longsuffering is the missionaries' own, displayed 'in me', so that they become good examples to the Lamanites. The Book of Mormon has kept the sentence's machinery — patience shown forth in a person for the sake of future believers — and moved the patience from the Saviour to the servants, which is precisely the theology of the verse's second half, where the Lord promises to make an instrument of them. Paul's point is that the chief of sinners is exhibit A; Alma's is that the preacher is.

links.note: 'Yet ye shall be patient in long suffering and afflictions, that ye may shew forth good examples unto them in me.' A KJV singleton's two halves with its purpose clause and its 'in me'. The one substitution is Paul's 'pattern' for the Book of Mormon's 'good examples', which is the same idea in plainer English. The 1830's open 'long suffering' was hyphenated in 1920; the KJV writes it solid, so no edition of the Book of Mormon has the source's orthography here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the hearts of the sons of Mosiah, and also those which were with them, took courage to go forth unto the Lamanites, to declare unto them the word of God.

And it came to pass when they had arriven in the borders of the land of the Lamanites, that they separated themselves, and departed one from another, trusting in the Lord, that they should meet again at the close of their harvest: for they supposed that great was the work which they had undertaken.—

And assuredly it was great, for they had undertaken to preach the word of God to a wild, and a hardened, and a ferocious people; a people which delighted in the murdering the Nephites, and robbing, and plundering them; and their hearts were set upon riches, or upon gold, and silver, and precious stones; yet they sought to obtain these things by murdering and plundering, that they might not labor for them with their own hands:

links.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.other: Psalm 62:10 contains two KJV singletons: "become not vain in robbery" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse and "set not your heart upon them" occurs in exactly 1, both this verse. It is the King James Bible's one sentence that puts robbery, increasing riches and a heart set on them into a single prohibition. Separately, "gold and silver and precious stones" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 18:12, and the triad appears exactly once in the 1830 Book of Mormon, here.
provenance.significance: The verse is Psalm 62:10 read as a description instead of a warning.
